TINYPUMPER BRAND FILE
GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT BY HAND

Source of truth for anyone, human or AI, building something that looks or sounds
like TinyPumper. Everything below is compiled from the owner docs listed under
PROVENANCE. Each rule lives in exactly one owner doc. To change a rule, change it
at its owner and rebuild this file with:

    python3 Mission_Control/scripts/build-brand-llm.py

Built: 2026-09-11
Human version of this file: https://tinypumper.com/brand/

HOW TO USE THIS FILE
--------------------
Paste the whole thing into your AI tool before asking it to design a page, write
an ad, draft an email, or generate an image for TinyPumper. It carries the exact
color tokens, type scale, layout system, imagery rules, voice laws, kill list,
value equation, guarantees, positioning doctrine, and the hard nos.

THE SHORT VERSION
-----------------
TinyPumper is 24/7 remote well monitoring that installs in 10 minutes. A
matchbox-sized solar-powered gateway plus radar tank, pressure and runtime
sensors, cellular or satellite included, flat rate per site with unlimited
sensors. It delivers roughly 99% of SCADA's upside without the cost or the
complexity, and it feeds straight into the Greasebook dashboard.

Positioning statement (alignment tool, not publication copy):
  For producers running conventional wells where SCADA never penciled or where
  aging SCADA costs more to keep alive than it returns, TinyPumper is the remote
  monitoring system that delivers roughly 99% of SCADA's upside without the cost
  or complexity. Unlike six-figure SCADA installs or telemetry that needs
  babysitting, TinyPumper self-installs in 10 minutes, runs solar with
  cellular/satellite included, one flat rate per site, 60-day money-back with
  lifetime sensor replacement.

Visual system in one breath:
  Warm cream #FAF8F5 and warm black #1C1B18, one gold accent #C8993B and nothing
  else. Libre Baskerville (400 and 700) for headings, Outfit (300-700) for
  everything else. 8px radius, UPPERCASE buttons in gold with dark text, 1080px
  container. Light theme only: dark is for contrast sections, never whole pages.

Voice in one breath:
  Talk like a peer, not a vendor. Picture an operator across a diner table in
  Midland with 20 minutes to spare. Plain words, short sentences, 8th grade or
  below. Show the moment, not the benefit. Prove it with numbers instead of
  adjectives. No em dashes, ever.

The brand name is written "TinyPumper": camel case, one word, capital T and
capital P. Not Tinypumper, not Tiny Pumper, not TINYPUMPER.

TWO TRAPS SPECIFIC TO THIS BRAND
--------------------------------
1. Never make a price admission. TinyPumper IS the cheap option, roughly 95%
   cheaper than SCADA, so "we're not the cheapest" is factually false here. The
   honest admission is that it watches rather than controls: no shut-ins, no
   pump adjustments, but ~99% of what you'd pay SCADA for.
2. Never use market-leader language ("the industry standard", "#1"). TinyPumper
   is mid-chasm; pragmatists check, and one caught overclaim poisons the
   reference chain. Claim product facts and guarantees, not throne-room language.

TinyPumper's guarantee is 60-day money-back plus lifetime sensor replacement.
Never borrow Greasebook's 200% guarantee, 6% lift, 98% success rate, or the
under-10-minute training claim. And never gate TinyPumper by well count: the
value prop holds for a 50-well operator and a 5,000-well operator alike.

PART 1 - VISUAL SYSTEM

## 1. Source of truth

| Surface | File | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Homepage `:root` | `tinypumper-deploy/index.html` | **Canonical.** Every token originates here. |
| PPC landers | `tinypumper-deploy/ppc/` | Must match. `ppc/template-lite.html` is the lean starting point. |
| Competitor pages | `tinypumper-deploy/vs/` | Must match |
| Quiz | `tp-quiz-deploy/` | TinyPumper system |

**There is no build step.** This repo is plain static HTML: what is committed is what ships. Every page carries its own `<style>` block, so a token change means touching each page rather than one stylesheet.

### GitHub Pages surface map

| Repo | Domain | Runs this system |
|---|---|---|
| `tinypumper-deploy` | `www.tinypumper.com` | Yes. **Source of truth.** |
| `tp-quiz-deploy` | `quiz.tinypumper.com` | Yes |
| `greasebook-deploy` | `www.greasebook.com` | No. See [`greasebook-design-system.md`](greasebook-design-system.md). |
| `gb-quiz-deploy` | `quiz.greasebook.com` | No. GreaseBook system. |

### Two hard rules that fail the deploy

- **Engagement beacon (Greg, 2026-08-14).** Every published HTML page loads `<script src="/assets/js/tp-attr.js"></script>` directly before `</head>`. There is no layout to inherit it from, so it goes in every page file. `.github/workflows/beacon-gate.yml` fails the deploy on any page missing it. Only meta-refresh redirect stubs are exempt. WHY: `tp-attr.js` feeds the `lander_engagement` telemetry that keyword scoring, the traffic-quality digest, and paid-ads cut/hold decisions read. A page without it is invisible to engagement scoring, and deep-read rate is a first-class optimization signal.
- **Assets are FILES, never base64 (Greg, 2026-08-18).** Every image and video is referenced as `../shared/<content-hash>.<ext>`. Never inline a `data:image/...;base64,` or `data:video/...;base64,` URI. WHY: 149 of 216 live `/ppc/` pages were 16.5 MB each because three MP4s were base64-inlined, so the browser had to download all of it before rendering anything, on pages we pay for clicks to, often on rural mobile. Fixed 2026-08-18: 2.4 GB down to 34 MB, each page 16.5 MB down to ~103 KB. Enforced by `.github/workflows/ppc-page-gate.yml`, which also blocks `\g<1>` regex artifacts and unrendered `{{ placeholder }}`.

**Deploys happen on `git push`.**

## 2. Name and wordmark

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| In body copy | **TinyPumper**. Camel case, one word, capital T and capital P. |
| Logo wordmark | Lowercase script, `tinypumper`, with a lightning bolt replacing the `y` stem. Never retype it. |
| Tagline | "the power to profit." Lowercase, with the full stop. It is part of the logo artwork, not live text. |
| Never | `Tinypumper`, `Tiny Pumper`, `TINYPUMPER` in body copy, or the wordmark set in a live font. |

Unlike GreaseBook, TinyPumper's spelling has never drifted: the site uses `TinyPumper` consistently.

---

## 3. Logo and mark

**The logo is a self-contained badge**: a black hexagonal shield with a gold-yellow outline, the `tinypumper` script inside, and the tagline beneath. Because the black field is part of the artwork, the badge sits on any background without a reversed variant.

| Asset | File | Format | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary badge** | `tinypumper-deploy/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/logo_yellow.svg` | SVG, viewBox `0 0 375 225` | **Default everywhere.** True vector, 37 paths, no embedded raster. |
| Marketing copy | `Mission_Control/docs/Infrastructure/assets/tinypumper-marketing/tinypumper-logo.svg` | SVG | Same artwork, decks and marketing |

### Rules

- The badge is **atomic**. Never separate the script from the shield, never drop the tagline, never re-colour the shield.
- Never place the badge on a busy photograph. Its own black field gives it contrast, but a photo behind the gold outline kills it.
- Clear space: at least the height of the lowercase `t` on all sides.
- Never stretch, skew, outline, or add shadows.
- TinyPumper **has genuine vector source art**, which GreaseBook did not. Always use the SVG. Never export a raster and ship that.

> **OPEN ITEM (raised 2026-09-11, needs Greg):** the logo artwork's yellow is **`#FFDE59`**, a bright lemon yellow. The brand gold used across the entire site UI is **`#C8993B`**, a deeper antique gold. They are not the same colour and both are in production, exactly like GreaseBook's two teals.
>
> This is not necessarily a bug: a brighter yellow reads better inside a small black badge than the muted UI gold would. But it should be a decision rather than an accident.
>
> Until Greg calls it: **build UI with `#C8993B` and leave the logo file alone.** Do not "correct" either one, and do not sample the logo's yellow for a button.

---

## 4. Color

The brand lives on a warm cream ground with a single gold accent, plus a near-black for contrast sections. Warm, not cool: every neutral has yellow in it. This is what separates TinyPumper from GreaseBook's cool off-white and near-black.

### Tokens (exact, from the homepage `:root`)

| Token | Hex | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--gold` | `#C8993B` | The accent. CTAs, highlights, emphasis, active states. |
| `--gold-hover` | `#B58A2F` | Button and link hover |
| `--gold-light` | `rgba(200,153,59,0.12)` | Soft gold fill behind accent elements |
| `--gold-highlight` | `rgba(200,153,59,0.15)` | Highlighted phrase background |
| `--bg` | `#FAF8F5` | Warm cream page background |
| `--bg-warm` | `#F3EFE9` | Alternate section background |
| `--bg-card` | `#FFFFFF` | Card and panel backgrounds |
| `--bg-dark` | `#1C1B18` | Nav, social proof, contrast sections |
| `--bg-dark-mid` | `#26241F` | Raised panel inside a dark section |
| `--ink` | `#1C1B18` | Primary text |
| `--ink-light` | `#FAF8F5` | Text on dark |
| `--ink-muted` | `#78736B` | Secondary text on light |
| `--ink-muted-lt` | `#A8A29E` | Secondary text on dark |
| `--ink-muted-lt-aa` | `#BDB8B2` | Secondary text on dark where AA contrast is required |
| `--green` | `#4D7C5A` | Success, guarantee, approval |
| `--red` | `#994848` | Urgency, warnings, the old way |
| `--border` | `#E2DDD5` | Card borders, dividers on light |
| `--border-dk` | `#3A3730` | Dividers on dark |
| Logo yellow | `#FFDE59` | **Logo artwork only.** Never in UI. See the open item above. |

### Rules

- **One accent.** Gold is the only accent. Green and red are status colours, not brand colours.
- **Never use GreaseBook teal (`#51A69D`) in a TinyPumper layout.** Two brands, two systems.
- **Never put two brand accents in one image.**
- **No dark-theme pages.** TinyPumper pages use the warm cream light theme. Dark is for specific contrast sections (nav, testimonials, proof bands), not whole pages.
- Card shadow is warm too: `rgba(28,27,24,0.06)`, never a neutral grey shadow.
- Reference every colour as a CSS custom property. Never hardcode a hex inline.

---

## 5. Typography

Two families do all the work. There is no third font.

| Family | Weights | Role | Fallback |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Libre Baskerville** | 400, 700, italic 400 | Headings (h1 to h3), pull quotes, big numbers | `Georgia, serif` |
| **Outfit** | 300, 400, 500, 600, 700 | Body, UI, buttons, labels, nav, captions | `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, sans-serif` |

Google Fonts load:

```
https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Libre+Baskerville:ital,wght@0,400;0,700;1,400&family=Outfit:wght@300;400;500;600;700&display=swap
```

### Scale

| Element | Setting |
|---|---|
| Body | `17px` / line-height `1.7` / Outfit 400 |
| Hero subhead | `clamp(17px, 2.5vw, 21px)` / line-height `1.55` / muted-light on dark |
| h3 | `22px` / Libre Baskerville **700** / margin-bottom `12px` |
| Buttons | `16px` / Outfit 600 / uppercase / letter-spacing `0.02em` |

### Rules

- **Max weight is 700.** Libre Baskerville supports 400/700, Outfit 300 to 700. Never 800 or 900.
- **Serif headlines, sans body.** No mixing in Inter, system fonts, or any other typeface.
- Headings use Libre Baskerville **700**, unlike GreaseBook where the display face has a single 400 weight. Do not carry GreaseBook's "never bold the display face" rule across: here bold is correct.
- Buttons are **uppercase**. GreaseBook's are not. This is a real difference between the two systems.

## 6. Layout and spacing

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--sec` | `120px` | Section padding, desktop |
| `--sec-m` | `72px` | Section padding, mobile |
| `--gutter` | `24px` | Horizontal gutter |
| `--max-w` | `1080px` | Content container |
| `--r-sm` | `4px` | Small chips, tags |
| `--r-md` | `8px` | **Standard.** Buttons, cards, panels |
| `--r-lg` | `16px` | Large cards, media frames |

Note the narrower container than GreaseBook (1080px vs 1200px) and the larger section rhythm (120px vs 80/100/120px).

---

## 7. Components

### Primary CTA

```css
.cta {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 8px;
  padding: 16px 36px;
  font-family: var(--f-body);      /* Outfit */
  font-size: 16px;
  font-weight: 600;
  color: var(--bg-dark);           /* dark text on gold */
  background: var(--gold);         /* #C8993B */
  border: none;
  border-radius: var(--r-md);      /* 8px */
  letter-spacing: .02em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  transition: background .2s, transform .15s;
}
.cta:hover { background: var(--gold-hover); transform: translateY(-1px); }
```

**No pill-shaped buttons (999px radius) and no gradient glow effects.** Gold background, dark text, 8px radius, uppercase, Outfit.

### Component vocabulary

- **Card:** `#FFFFFF` fill, `#E2DDD5` border, warm shadow `rgba(28,27,24,0.06)`, `8px` or `16px` radius.
- **Section rhythm:** `.section--dark` (`#1C1B18`) and `.section--warm` (`#F3EFE9`) alternate against the cream default. The hero is dark.
- **Highlighted phrase:** `--gold-highlight` background behind the words that matter.

## 8. Imagery, as TinyPumper applies it

The imagery system is owned by `~/.claude/skills/seo-content-operator/references/imagery-system.md`. Load it before generating or placing any image. Only the TinyPumper-specific bindings live here:

- **Brand accent in illustrations: gold `#C8993B`.** Neutral warm base plus that single accent.
- **Never gold and GreaseBook teal in the same image.**
- **Real field photography is the strength here.** TinyPumper has a large library of actual installed-hardware photos from real leases. Use them. This is the one place where photography beats illustration by default, because the product is physical and the install claim ("10 minutes, no trenching") is proved by seeing it on a real tank.
- Product shots must show the **actual gear**: matchbox-sized gateway, radar tank sensor on top of a tank, pressure sensor at the wellhead, turbine meter inline.

### Approved asset libraries

| Library | Contents | Approved use |
|---|---|---|
| `tinypumper-field-images/` | ~100 real install photos from customer leases | Install proof, hero, section imagery |
| `tinypumper-marketing/` | Gateway product shots, pressure sensor, app screens, hero images, QR, logo SVG | Product demonstration |
| `tinypumper-client-proof/` | Customer-supplied install photos | Social proof |
| `as-seen-on-logos/` | Rigzone, SPE, The OGM, Oil & Gas Financial Journal, E&P Magazine, American Oil & Gas Reporter, OilVoice | Press credibility bar |

**Never show a competitor's hardware.** And never stage a photo that implies we did the install: the client self-installs, which is the whole claim.

---

## 9. What must never cross from GreaseBook

TinyPumper and GreaseBook share a buyer, a voice, and a dashboard. They share nothing visual, and they sit on **opposite sides of the chasm**, so they need opposite proof.

| | TinyPumper | GreaseBook |
|---|---|---|
| Accent | Gold `#C8993B` | Teal `#51A69D` |
| Ground | Warm cream `#FAF8F5` | Cool off-white `#FAFAF9` |
| Dark | `#1C1B18` (warm black) | `#0F1114` (cool black) |
| Display font | Libre Baskerville, 400 **and 700** | DM Serif Display, **400 only** |
| Body font | Outfit | DM Sans |
| Buttons | **Uppercase**, 8px radius | Sentence case, 6px radius |
| Container | 1080px | 1200px |
| Chasm stage | **Mid-chasm.** Triangulation and references. | Across it. Leadership and safety proof. |
| Guarantee | 60-day money-back **plus lifetime sensor replacement** | 200% money-back |
| Damaging admission | "It watches, it doesn't control." | "We're not the cheapest option out there." |

**Two TinyPumper-specific traps:**

1. **Never make a price admission for TinyPumper.** TinyPumper IS the cheap option: roughly 95% cheaper than SCADA. "We're not the cheapest" is factually false here, and Greg caught exactly that on a lander (2026-07-22). TinyPumper's honest admission is that it monitors rather than controls: no shut-ins, no pump adjustments, but ~99% of what you'd pay SCADA for.
2. **Never use unearned market-leader language** ("the industry standard", "#1"). TinyPumper is mid-chasm; pragmatists check, and one caught overclaim poisons the reference chain. It claims product facts and guarantees, not throne-room language, until the reference base earns it.

The four GreaseBook-only numbers that must never appear on a TinyPumper surface: **6% pump-to-net in 6 weeks, 98% success rate, 200% money-back, and the under-10-minute pumper training claim.**

================================================================================
PART 2 - VOICE
================================================================================

## Who We're Talking To

**Primary audience:** Small-to-mid-size oil & gas operators
- Often owner-operators running 10-500 wells
- Built their business with sweat, not spreadsheets
- Been burned by software that overpromised and underdelivered
- Skeptical of salespeople, allergic to corporate speak
- Value practical solutions over fancy features
- Time-poor — they've got wells to check, payroll to run, and a hundred fires to put out

**Secondary audience:** Pumpers and field hands
- Blue collar, boots-on-the-ground workers
- Not "tech people" — they want tools that just work
- Pride in their craft, loyal to operators who respect them
- Many are ESL speakers

**Geography & culture:** Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, North Dakota — oil patch through and through. These folks can spot a slick marketing pitch from a mile away, and they'll tune it out just as fast.

---

## The Core Principle

**We talk like a peer, not a vendor.**

Imagine you're sitting across from an operator at a diner in Midland. Coffee's hot, he's got 20 minutes before he needs to be somewhere. How would you explain what Greasebook or TinyPumper does?

You wouldn't say "leverage our cloud-based solution to optimize your production workflows."

You'd say "Your pumper calls in sick tomorrow (or doesn't call at all...) Do you know what happened on your wells yesterday?"

That's the voice.

---

## The 7 Laws of External Copy

### 1. Plain Words, Short Sentences

Write like you talk. If you wouldn't say it out loud to an operator, don't write it.

| Don't Write | Write Instead |
|-------------|---------------|
| "Optimize your production reporting workflow" | "Know what's happening on your wells" |
| "Leverage real-time data analytics" | "See your tanks right now, from anywhere" |
| "Our solution integrates seamlessly" | "It works with what you've already got" |
| "Utilize our platform to maximize efficiency" | "Spend less time on paperwork" |

**Reading level:** 8th grade or below. Simple words, short sentences, no jargon. Use the Hemingway App. If it flags a sentence, rewrite it.

### 2. Show the Moment, Not the Benefit

Don't tell them they'll "save time" or "reduce costs." Show them the exact moment they'll feel the difference.

| Abstract Benefit | The Moment |
|------------------|------------|
| "Save time on reporting" | "Your pumper taps 'submit' and you see the gauge reading before he's back in his truck" |
| "Reduce theft and losses" | "You're watching the tank level drop at 2am when nobody should be on that lease" |
| "Better communication" | "No more calling three pumpers to find out why production's down" |
| "Peace of mind" | "You're at your kid's baseball game and you check your wells from the bleachers" |

**Ask yourself:** What's the specific moment when they'll realize this is working? Describe that moment.

### 3. Acknowledge the Skepticism

Our prospects have been sold to. A lot. They've bought software that promised the moon and delivered headaches. They've sat through demos that looked great and products that didn't work in the field.

**Use damaging admissions to build trust:**

- "We're not the cheapest option out there." **(GreaseBook contexts only — NEVER for TinyPumper: TP IS the cheapest, its whole pitch is 95% cheaper than SCADA; a price admission there is factually false. Greg caught it on a lander 2026-07-22. TP's true admission is "it watches, it doesn't control" — no shut-ins, no pump adjustments, but 99% of what you'd pay SCADA for.)**
- "This won't replace your pumper — it makes him better."
- "If you've only got 5 wells, you probably don't need this yet."
- "The first week, your guys might grumble about it. By week three, they won't want to go back."

**Structure:** [Honest limitation] + **but** + [Benefit you want them to believe]

The statement after "but" is what sticks. What you sacrifice in promise, you gain in trust. And trust is everything with this audience.

### 4. Prove It, Don't Claim It

Operators trust proof, not promises. They've heard "best in class" and "industry-leading" a thousand times.

**Weak (claims):**
- "The best production software in the industry"
- "Trusted by operators everywhere"
- "Revolutionary technology"

**Strong (proof):**
- "600+ production companies. 10,000+ pumpers. 15 years in the oil patch."
- "87 five-star reviews on Capterra — read 'em yourself."
- "The fastest growing oil and gas production software in the patch today."

**Specificity = credibility.** Numbers, names, facts. If you can't prove it, don't say it.

### 5. Respect Their Time

These folks are busy. They're not reading your email for fun. Get to the point.

- **Emails:** Under 150 words for cold outreach. Say what you want in the first two sentences.
- **Landing pages:** Lead with the payoff. Don't make them scroll to find out what you do.
- **Ads:** 3 seconds to hook them. No buildup, no throat-clearing.

**Delete these phrases:**
- "I hope this email finds you well"
- "I wanted to reach out because..."
- "I'd love the opportunity to..."
- "At [Company], we believe..."

Just say the thing.

### 6. Oilfield Flavor — Authentic, Not Hokey

We're not putting on a costume. We're not writing "y'all" in every sentence or dropping fake cowboy slang to seem relatable.

But we do speak the language:
- "Lease" not "site"
- "Pumper" not "field technician"
- "Gauge" not "measure"
- "Run tickets" not "delivery documentation"
- "Stripper wells" — we know what they are and we're not scared to say it

**The test:** Would an operator in Odessa roll his eyes at this? If yes, cut it.

### 7. Confident, Not Arrogant

We've been doing this for 15 years. We know our product works. We don't need to brag or oversell.

**Arrogant:** "The only production software you'll ever need"
**Confident:** "We've been doing this since 2009. We've seen what works."

**Arrogant:** "Our competitors can't match our technology"
**Confident:** "Ask our customers why they switched. We'll give you their numbers."

**Arrogant:** "You need this"
**Confident:** "This might not be for everyone. But if you're running 50+ wells and your pumper's handwriting gives you nightmares, let's talk."

---

## Voice by Channel

### Cold Email
- **Spirit:** Hormozi + Halbert
- Under 100 words
- One clear ask
- No pitching in the first line — lead with a question or observation about their world
- Sound like a person, not a company

### Landing Pages
- **Spirit:** Hormozi + Brunson
- Headline = the moment they'll experience, not the feature
- Damaging admission in the first scroll
- Proof (numbers, testimonials) before the CTA
- One action per page

### Ads (Social/Digital)
- **Spirit:** Hormozi + Caples
- 3-second hook — get to the point
- Show the moment, not the benefit
- Call out who it's NOT for (specificity attracts)
- No marketing lingo

### Sales Emails / Follow-ups
- **Spirit:** Halbert + Hopkins
- Personal, conversational
- Reference something specific about them
- P.S. line with the core benefit restated
- Never sound desperate

### Website / Brand Copy
- **Spirit:** Ogilvy + Godin (for positioning), Hormozi (for conversion pages)
- Lead with who you help, not what you do
- Proof and credibility front and center
- Let testimonials do the heavy lifting

---

## Words We Use / Words We Don't

### Kill List (Never Use)
| Word/Phrase | Why |
|-------------|-----|
| "Revolutionary" | Everyone says it. Means nothing. |
| "Best-in-class" | Prove it or cut it. |
| "Leverage" | Corporate speak. Say "use." |
| "Optimize" | Vague. Say what actually improves. |
| "Seamless" | Nobody believes this. |
| "Robust" | Tech jargon. |
| "Solution" | Say what it actually is. |
| "Synergy" | Just don't. |
| "Empower" | Show the result instead. |
| "I hope this finds you well" | Wasted words. |
| Em dashes in copy | Dead giveaway of LLM output. Use parens, periods, or colons instead. |

### Email Format Rules — Greg's Law (prospect-facing email ONLY)

Every email a prospect receives (macros, Quick Replies, campaign sequences, automated follow-ups, one-off unibox replies) follows these rules. **Why:** Greg's direct feedback, twice — 2026-06-17 ("no paragraph should be longer then 1 sentence... space bt each paragraph for readability... note there shouldn't be a space bt the name and the comma") and 2026-01-09 ("people are becoming aware of GPT created messages and they do NOT like them. Stay away from Bolding words and em dashes"). Updated 2026-08-02: PS block exception. Revisit only if Greg changes the call.

- **One sentence per paragraph. Maximum.** Blank line between every paragraph.
- **PS exception:** The P.S. is never broken into separate paragraphs. Keep the full PS as one block. If the PS is 2–3 short sentences, they stay in that single paragraph (do not put a blank line between PS sentences). Longer than ~3 sentences: cut the PS down; do not multi-paragraph it.
- **"Winston," never "Winston ,"** — no space before the comma after the name.
- **No bold anywhere in the body.** No em dashes (already on the kill list).
- **No background colors** — clear formatting before sending.
- These are EMAIL rules. Landing pages, ads, and docs keep their own formatting rules from this guide.

### Craft Rules
- **Proper Case all names.** Pumper names, operator names, executive names. "John Smith", never "JOHN SMITH" or "john smith". No exceptions.
- **Copy length:** no word counts. Every sentence earns its spot. If it does new work, it stays. Long copy is fine. Fluff is not.
- **Second person.** Write in "you", not "they" or "our customers". Makes it personal. The reader is the operator sitting across the diner table.
- **Short paragraphs.** 1 to 3 sentences max. White space is a feature, not a waste of pixels.
- **Bold the key phrases.** Let the reader skim and still get the point. The eye should land on the thing that matters without having to read the full paragraph.
- **Explain oilfield expressions for ESL readers.** Many readers (pumpers, field hands, teammates on the back office and support side) speak English as a second language. When you use an oilfield quip or regional expression, add a parenthetical so everyone gets it. Example: "That dog won't hunt (meaning: that idea won't work)."
- **Acknowledge that it's hard. Then set clear expectations.** Real work is hard. Don't pretend it isn't. Name the friction, then tell the reader exactly what to expect. "The first week your pumpers might grumble. By week three they won't want to go back." is stronger than "seamless rollout."

### Replacements
| Instead of... | Say... |
|---------------|--------|
| "Our platform enables you to..." | "You can..." |
| "We provide a solution for..." | "This does..." |
| "Significant ROI" | "Pays for itself in [X]" |
| "Streamline your operations" | "Less paperwork" or "Fewer phone calls" |
| "Data-driven insights" | "You'll see exactly what's happening" |
| "Cutting-edge technology" | [Just describe what it does] |

---

## Quick Gut-Check

Before publishing any external copy, ask:

1. **Would I say this out loud to an operator?** If it sounds weird spoken, rewrite it.
2. **Is there a moment?** Or am I just listing features and benefits?
3. **Where's the proof?** Claims without evidence get ignored.
4. **Did I acknowledge the skepticism?** What's the damaging admission?
5. **Can I cut 20%?** Probably yes. Do it.
6. **Would an Odessa operator roll his eyes?** If yes, too slick. Dial it back.

---

## The Bottom Line

We're not selling software. We're selling peace of mind to people who've got enough to worry about.

Talk to them straight. Show them you understand their world. Prove you can help. Respect their time.

That's it.

---
================================================================================
PART 3 - AI TELLS TO STRIP
================================================================================

These are the fingerprints of AI-generated content. Every one erodes trust with an industry reader. The QA gate must flag any of these.

## Sentence Openers to Ban
- "In today's digital era" / "In today's fast-paced world" / "In an era of"
- "When it comes to"
- "It's worth noting that" / "It's important to note that"
- "In conclusion" / "To conclude" / "To sum up" / "In summary"
- "As we navigate" / "As we move forward"
- "Let's dive into" / "Let's explore" / "Let's unpack"

## Transition Words to Ban
- "Furthermore" / "Moreover" / "Additionally" / "In addition"
- "Notably" / "Importantly" / "Significantly"
- "Indeed" (unless used sparingly and naturally)

## Banned Verbs / Phrases
- "Delve into" / "Delve deeper"
- "Navigate the landscape"
- "Landscape" (when describing an industry/market)
- "Leverage" (when "use" works)
- "Unlock" (as in "unlock insights", "unlock potential")
- "Game-changer" / "Game-changing"
- "Revolutionize" / "Revolutionary"
- "Cutting-edge" / "State-of-the-art"
- "Seamless" / "Seamlessly"
- "Holistic" (unless clinically correct)
- "Robust" (overused)
- "Comprehensive" (usually filler)
- "Tailored" / "Bespoke"
- "Embark on a journey"
- "Harness the power of"
- "Elevate your [noun]"
- "Empower"
- "Transformative"

## Structural Tells
- Three-item lists where everything is alliterative or parallel to the point of pattern ("efficient, effective, and empowering")
- Every paragraph ending with a one-sentence summary of itself
- H2s that are all gerund phrases ("Understanding X", "Exploring Y", "Navigating Z")
- Closing paragraphs that restate the intro
- Bullet lists where every item is the same length
- Perfect five-paragraph structure (intro, three body, conclusion)

## Punctuation Tells
- **Em dashes (—)**: dead giveaway. Use parentheses, a period, or a colon. Never em dashes.
- Curly quotes inside code blocks
- Oxford commas everywhere (not inherently bad but a pattern)

## Content Tells
- Paragraphs that warn about "potential challenges" without naming real ones
- Generic "best practices" that apply to any industry
- Made-up statistics (always cite a source or don't use the number)
- Qualifying everything ("often", "typically", "generally", "usually") — commits to nothing
- Restating the question before answering ("Great question! When it comes to…")
- Closing the article with "I hope this helps" or equivalent

## What Authentic Industry Writing Looks Like
- Specific numbers tied to real scenarios ("a 15-well stripper operation running 3 bpd per well")
- Named competitors, named products, named places
- A real anecdote or scenario (even if composite)
- Industry jargon used correctly without over-explaining
- An opinion that a competitor would disagree with
- Admitting limitations ("this won't help if you're running high-volume horizontals")
================================================================================
PART 4 - WHAT WE SAY
================================================================================

## 1. Who We Sell To

### Bright-Line Rule: The Buyer Is The Producer. Always.

For **both GreaseBook and TinyPumper**, the buyer is the **producer** — the operating company that owns the wells and signs the check. Never the pumper. Never the contract pumper.

Pumpers and contract pumpers are **users** of the tools. The producer is the buyer. Copy, ads, landing pages, sales pitches, and every piece of marketing must be aimed at the producer's job, the producer's pain, and the producer's P&L. Everything else is a feature.

- **Do not pitch TinyPumper as "for contract pumpers managing multiple operators."** Contract pumpers are not the buyer. The producer who hires them is. If a contract pumper is on the lease, TinyPumper is there because the *producer* bought it.
- **Do not frame GreaseBook as "a tool for pumpers."** Pumpers use the app because their employer (the producer) bought it. The pitch lives in the operator's economics and the operator's risk, not pumper convenience. Pumper-side benefits (shorter days, no paper) are a feature, not the thesis.
- **Do not segment copy by "operator vs contract pumper" as two buyer types.** There is one buyer type — the producer. Whether their field work is done by company pumpers or a contract pumping outfit is an implementation detail.
- **When in doubt, picture the reader.** The reader of any piece of marketing is an owner, operator, engineer, ops supervisor, or back-office admin inside a producing company. Write to them.

### The Company Profile

Independent oil and gas producers running anywhere from **2 to 2,000 wells**. Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Colorado, Kansas, North Dakota, Michigan, Appalachia, Illinois basin, California. Operators who built the business with sweat, not stock options. The wells Wall Street does not talk about but America still runs on.

These companies typically have:

- A small back office (1 to 10 people).
- Somewhere between 3 and 30 pumpers (company, contract, or a blend).
- Data flowing through paper gauge sheets, Excel spreadsheets, emails, texts, or a mix of all four.
- No SCADA (too expensive) OR legacy SCADA they are tired of paying to maintain.
- An owner or operations lead who knows their production numbers are 2 to 3 weeks behind reality.

### Well-Count Range — Do Not Cap the Upper End

Company profile is **2 to 2,000 wells**. Copy must reflect the full range. A meaningful slice of our book operates **1,000+ wells**, and plenty sit in the 1,000 to 2,000 band. We are comfortable serving them and we win business there.

- **Do not cap scene-setting at 500 wells.** Lines like "a 500-well operator", "a 50-well operation", "small independents with a few dozen wells" anchor the reader to the low end and tell every larger operator the article is not for them. They bounce.
- **Use ranges, not single numbers.** "15 to 500 wells", "a few dozen to a few thousand wells", "small and mid-size independents operating anywhere from a handful of wells to 2,000+" all keep the full audience in the room.
- **When a pillar is genuinely scoped small** (e.g., stripper-well specific page), the small anchor is fine — but that must match the target keyword, not be incidental scene-dressing.
- **Do not imply our upper limit is 500 or 1,000 wells.** We serve operators in excess of 1,000 wells and intend to keep serving them. The ceiling in copy is 2,000, not 500.

### Horizontal Well Operators — Not Alienated

GreaseBook serves a meaningful book of **horizontal well operators** and does it well. Copy must never imply GreaseBook is "for stripper / vertical ops only" or otherwise excommunicate the horizontal reader.

- **GreaseBook integrates with SCADA.** Horizontal operators running SCADA on their best wells plug GreaseBook into the same environment. Field-entered data, SCADA-sourced data, and exec dashboards live in one screen. GreaseBook is the centralized production source of truth regardless of how the data got there.
- **Product fit inside a horizontal op:** GreaseBook is the right fit when SCADA is already in play. GreaseBook lives alongside SCADA; it does not try to replace it.
- **TinyPumper is anti-SCADA by design.** TinyPumper's pitch is "if you were going to spend a bunch of money on SCADA, don't — there's TinyPumper." That is correct positioning for TinyPumper. But that positioning **does not** extend to GreaseBook, and it **does not** mean horizontal operators are not welcome. The choice inside a horizontal shop is usually: keep SCADA + add GreaseBook for the production layer, or replace low-value SCADA installs with TinyPumper.
- **Simple rule for any article:** if the copy knocks SCADA in a way that could read as "GreaseBook is not for you if you run SCADA," rewrite. GreaseBook is absolutely for them.

### The Buyer Personas (Role-Based)

Different roles inside the same company care about different things. Match the pitch to the person on the other end of the line.

| Role | Core Focus | What They Care About | How We Pitch Them |
|------|-----------|----------------------|-------------------|
| **Owner** | A holistic business solution | Profit, transparency, accountability, employee oversight | High-level view: how GreaseBook lifts margin across the whole operation |
| **Engineer** | Clean, quality-controlled data | PHDwin integration, custom reports, Alert Engine, API | Technical depth, but tie every feature back to a problem it solves |
| **Operations Supervisor** | Simplicity for pumpers | Basic reports, scheduled reports, ease of use | Time-saving for the field team, not executive dashboards |
| **Office Admin** | Automating tedious work | State reports, scheduled reports, custom reports | We automate the stuff that keeps them at their desk past 5 |
| **Pumper** | Getting off the route faster | No paperwork, no phone calls, no mail-in tickets | Shorter days, less hassle, weekends back |

### The Pain Profile (What Brings Them To Us)

Pulled from hundreds of discovery calls. This is what operators tell us, in their own words:

- "We need a centralized system for production reporting, taxes, and reconciliations. Managing Excel sheets is overwhelming."
- "Our pumpers mail in tickets, and we are at the mercy of the mail system. We need real-time access to data."
- "I want to streamline operations, eliminate paper processes, and make field data accessible in one place."
- "With oil back at $60 a barrel, we need a tool to optimize our operations and capitalize on this price."
- "We want to go digital from the start and simplify our production data management."

The common threads:

1. **Data is late.** Most operators are running 2 to 3 weeks behind on production numbers.
2. **Data is messy.** Paper, Excel, text, email. Nothing ties together.
3. **Pumpers are a black box.** No way to verify they showed up, no way to catch issues they missed.
4. **Back office is drowning.** State reports, run ticket reconciliation, and tax filings eat hours every week.
5. **SCADA is too expensive for marginal wells.** Big wells may get SCADA. The rest fly blind.

## 2. What Each Product Does

### GreaseBook (the Production App)

**In one sentence:** GreaseBook gets production data from your pumper's phone to your screen, instantly. No paper. No Excel. No chasing anyone down.

**What it is:** A two-sided software platform.

1. **The Pumper App** (iOS and Android). Pumpers log daily gauges, pressures, comments, run tickets, and photos. Works offline, auto-syncs when back in cell range. Geo-fencing confirms the pumper actually stepped foot on the lease. Learning curve is about 8 minutes. If the pumper can text, he can use GreaseBook.
2. **The Executive Dashboard.** Owners, engineers, and office staff see live production, custom reports, state reports, alert engine, well history files, allocations, downtime tracker, and PHDwin integration. Think of it as mission control for the whole operation.

**Setup:** Turnkey. We build the company out. Client sends tank sizes, well names, and pumper contact info. A production engineer handles the rest. Average pumper onboarding is a half day of training, done for you. Average office user is 99% proficient in about 20 minutes.

**State Report Coverage (rule updated by Greg, 2026-07-11):** GreaseBook auto-files state production reports for **any oil and gas producing state**. On the rare chance a state's form isn't already built, GreaseBook builds it **at no cost to the operator** — "because if you need it, there's a good chance somebody else is going to need it" (Greg). **Copy rule: NEVER enumerate a short list of states as if it were the coverage** — naming TX/MS/AL/WY/MI reads as "we don't do Kansas/Oklahoma/Colorado" by negative space. The free-build promise is what makes the any-state claim honest. (Supersedes the fixed five-state list that stood here until 2026-07-11; revisit only if the free-build policy changes.)

When writing any article, pillar, or page that touches state production reporting, the Texas report may be the headline (it is the biggest market), but **the copy must never imply Texas is the only state we support.** Name the full list, or use a phrase like "Texas and a growing set of other states including Mississippi, Alabama, Wyoming, and Michigan." Do not write copy that excommunicates operators in MS, AL, WY, or MI.

**What it replaces:** Paper gauge sheets, Excel workbooks, Dropbox folders, group texts, email chains, and in some cases competing platforms like iWell, FieldDirect, Productioneer (Mi4), Wolfpack, and others.

**Pricing anchor:** Based on well count and operator complexity. Quiz at `quiz.greasebook.com` returns a custom quote in 60 seconds.

### TinyPumper (the Remote Monitoring Hardware)

**In one sentence:** TinyPumper is 24/7 remote well monitoring that installs in 10 minutes. No wires. No SCADA. No kidding.

**What it is:** A matchbox-sized, solar-powered gateway plus radar and pressure sensors.

- **Gateway** connects up to 8 sensors over Bluetooth and pushes data to the cloud over cellular or satellite. Solar powered. IP67-rated. Class I Div 1 certified. Built-in shake counter detects whether an engine or compressor is running.
- **Radar tank sensor** mounts on top of a tank. No fluid contact, no corrosion, no gunk, no freezing.
- **Pressure sensor** at the wellhead, flowline, or injection well.
- **Turbine meter** integration available.

**What it monitors:**

- Tank levels (oil, water, saltwater disposal).
- Pressures (wellhead, flowline, injection).
- Engine and compressor runtime (uptime monitoring).

**It is not** just a tank monitor. It is a full site monitor.

**Install:** The client self-installs in about 8 to 10 minutes. No electrician, no trenching, no third-party service call. If you can change a lightbulb, you can install TinyPumper. (Never say "we install it." The client does.)

**Update frequency:** Sensor fires every hour (conserves battery). Between those reads, the sensor also wakes every 5 minutes to check threshold conditions. If something crosses the line, the gateway pushes an alert immediately, even outside the regular hourly report.

**Pricing:**

| Component | Price |
|-----------|-------|
| Hardware (cellular gateway, one-time) | $349 |
| Hardware (satellite gateway, one-time) | $549 |
| 3x per day polling (every 8 hours) | $79 / month |
| 6x per day polling (every 4 hours) | $99 / month |
| Hourly polling (cellular) | $129 / month |
| Hourly polling (satellite) | $149 / month |

Flat rate per site. Unlimited sensors at that location. Cellular connectivity included. No carrier bill, no dead zone worries, no setup fees, no training fees, no hidden charges.

**Temperature range:** -40°C to 70°C (-38°F to 158°F). Deployed in North Dakota, Canada, Wisconsin, and Alaska with no cold weather issues.

**What it replaces:** Legacy SCADA (eLynx, ZDScada, PetroPower, SignalFire), modern remote monitoring (iWell, Sensorfield, Innotech, Tank Sentinel, Amplified Industries, REIGN, Rulo, Tank to Cloud, Rugged Monitoring).

### TinyPumper Is Not Well-Count Gated — It Is The SCADA Alternative

**TinyPumper's fit is not about well count. It is about the economics and complexity of SCADA on conventional wells.** Commit this to memory before writing a single line about TinyPumper.

The whole point of TinyPumper is this: it delivers roughly **99% of the upside of SCADA without the cost or the complexity**. That value prop is true for a 50-well operator and a 5,000-well operator. Scale does not change the math.

Two scenarios where TinyPumper wins:

1. **The operator never put SCADA in because it was always too expensive.** The capex, the wiring, the IT burden, the ongoing maintenance — the ROI never penciled, so the wells run blind. TinyPumper unlocks monitoring they were priced out of.
2. **The operator has aging SCADA that is breaking down, and the cost to maintain it no longer justifies the upside.** Replacing sensors, servicing gear, paying hosts to babysit the stack. TinyPumper is the drop-in replacement that kills the maintenance drag.

Either scenario applies at **any scale**. A 50-well conventional operator and a 5,000-well conventional operator both buy TinyPumper for the same reason.

**What to never write for TinyPumper copy:**

- **"TinyPumper is for small operators."** False. Operators well above 1,000 wells use TinyPumper.
- **"Once you hit X wells, you need SCADA instead."** False. The SCADA threshold is about cost and complexity per site, not total well count. A 2,000-well operator running marginal conventional wells still finds SCADA uneconomic and still chooses TinyPumper.
- **"TinyPumper fits best between 5 and 50 wells."** False. Do not bucket TinyPumper into a well-count band. Any copy that tries to will alienate the larger operators who are already our customers.
- **"TinyPumper is the contract pumper's tool."** False. The producer is the buyer regardless of who does the field work. See Section 1 bright-line rule.

**The segmentation that actually matters for TinyPumper:** is this a conventional well (or conventional tank battery, or conventional facility) where SCADA is either breaking down or never got installed because the math never worked? If yes, TinyPumper fits — whether the operator runs 50 wells or 5,000.

### Together: GreaseBook + TinyPumper

The TinyPumper data flows straight into the GreaseBook executive dashboard. So an operator using both gets:

- Pumper-entered data (daily gauges, comments, run tickets).
- Sensor-automated data (tank levels, pressures, runtime).
- Alerts across both (pumper forgot to call in a tank, or pressure crossed a threshold at 2 a.m.).
- One screen. One source of truth. Same platform.

Operators running both typically see 50%+ fewer pumper site visits, a 10% production boost, and a meaningful number of field days freed up.

### The WolfePak acquisition story (approved for public use, Greg 2026-07-11)

## 6. Positioning Against Competitors

### Positioning Doctrine — Crossing the Chasm (Greg, 2026-07-14)

Three rules from Geoffrey Moore's *Crossing the Chasm* govern everything below and every piece of marketing this doc feeds. **WHY they live here:** our buyers are pragmatists and conservatives, the psychographics Moore's book is about. Pragmatists cannot evaluate a product in a vacuum; they buy by triangulating against things they already know, and they buy different proof depending on which side of the chasm the product is on. (Decided by Greg 2026-07-14 during the advertorial project; revisit if either brand's market stage changes.)

#### Rule 1 — Triangulate off two beacons, always

Moore's terms: the **market alternative** (the old way the buyer already spends money on; we steal its budget) and the **product alternative** (the incumbent technology; it proves the category exists while we differentiate against it). Copy that names only one beacon leaves the reader an exit. Naming only paper/Excel invites "fine, we'll buy the established software." Naming only the incumbent invites "fine, we'll stay on paper." Name both, and the natural landing point is ours by construction.

| Brand | Old way (market alternative) | Incumbent (product alternative) | Natural third point |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GreaseBook** | Paper gauge sheets, phone calls, a clerk retyping into Excel | Legacy production software: overpriced, overbuilt, parked on an office laptop, needs a clerk to feed it | The phone the pumper already carries. No new device, no training course. |
| **TinyPumper** | Flying blind between pumper visits; finding out when the run ticket is light | SCADA / legacy remote monitoring / telemetry (rotate the anchor term per the anchor-rotation rule): six-figure installs, IT to babysit, maintenance drag | Right-sized hardware the operator self-installs in 10 minutes, flat rate per site |

**Composition with the 2026-07-13 attack-lines rule (Section 8):** the two rules stack, they don't conflict. Triangulation says name both beacons **together** so the reader can't exit sideways. The attack-lines rule says each beacon gets attacked only with **its own** failure mode: Excel/paper fails on centralized visibility and double work; legacy software fails on lock-in, learning lift, and laptop-bound data entry. Never swap their failure modes, never name only one beacon. (Never name Pump Pilot.)

**The incumbent stays UNNAMED in general marketing copy (Greg, 2026-07-14, refined same day):** ads, advertorials, and the homepage describe the incumbent, never name it: "legacy production software, laptop-based, contract lock-in." **WHY:** naming a competitor hands the reader a name to go research and injects a third party into the sales conversation; the description is damning enough, and anyone actually running one of these systems knows exactly who we mean without the name. Named-competitor content is reserved for the surfaces built to name names: the competitor lander/SKAG program and sales calls. For those surfaces, the grounded reference list is **IHS FieldDirect** (primary: the most common incumbent prospects name on the "what do you use today" Typeform question, and "been around forever" per sales recon), **WolfePak** (old), and **Productioneer (Mi4)**. **iWell is a modern peer, NOT a legacy incumbent — never use it as the old-software beacon anywhere.**

**Excel is part of beacon one and gets its own failure modes (Greg, 2026-07-14):** the old-way beacon is paper AND Excel, and copy must touch both — never let Excel ride along implicitly under "paper." Excel's distinct failure modes: it's free and FEELS like software (digitized, centralized, backed up), which is exactly why operators trust it past its breaking point; the double entry survives (pumper still writes or texts, somebody still keys it in); version chaos (no single source of truth, per-route formats, FINAL_v3 files in inboxes); silent errors (bad sorts, fat-fingered cells, zero validation at the source). Paper's failure modes stay paper's (visibility, double work, accountability). House line: "Excel is paper with a power cord." **WHY:** a huge share of prospects sit on Excel believing they already modernized; copy that only attacks paper tells them the article isn't about them.

**"Free" is Excel's biggest lie — say so (Greg, 2026-07-14):** Excel's price isn't zero, it's invisible: it never sends an invoice. Copy attacking the Excel beacon should name the real costs in production terms: clerk hours keying the same numbers twice, downtime hiding in stale files, run tickets that won't reconcile, wells that slip while the truth sits in an inbox. What falls through the cracks IS the subscription fee. House lines: "the most expensive free software in the oil patch" / "Excel never sends an invoice." **WHY:** "it's free" is the exact reason operators park on Excel past its breaking point; leaving the price myth unchallenged leaves their strongest objection standing.

#### Rule 2 — Two brands, two sides of the chasm

**GreaseBook crossed the chasm years ago.** Its buyer pool now includes late-majority conservatives, who buy the safe, complete, market-leading choice. GB marketing leans **leadership-and-safety proof**: 600+ companies, 10,000+ pumpers, 15 years, 220 million barrels, top-rated on Capterra/G2, turnkey setup, the 200% guarantee. The GB failure mode is scrappy-underdog copy: it surrenders the exact proof a conservative needs and makes the safe choice sound risky.

**TinyPumper is mid-chasm right now.** Its game is the crossing playbook: named competition (the competitor lander/SKAG program), two-beacon triangulation, and peer references. The TP failure mode is unearned market-leader language ("the industry standard," "#1"): pragmatists check, and one caught overclaim poisons the reference chain we're trying to start. TP claims product facts and guarantees, not throne-room language, until the reference base earns it.

**WHY:** pragmatists and conservatives buy opposite proof (references and whole-product completeness vs. leadership and ubiquity). Copy that borrows the other brand's playbook works against the buyer's psychology, even when every individual claim in it is true.

#### Rule 3 — The two-sentence positioning statement (alignment tool, not publication copy)

Moore's formula: *For (target customer) who (compelling reason to buy), (product) is a (category) that (key benefit). Unlike (old way / incumbent), we (primary differentiation).* Every ad, lander, advertorial, and cold email should read as a paraphrase of its brand's statement. If a draft can't be traced back to it, the draft is off-position. The formula forces both beacons into every piece by construction.

**GreaseBook:** For independent producers (2 to 2,000 wells) who make decisions on production numbers that run two to three weeks behind the field, GreaseBook is the top-rated oil and gas production app that gets pumper data from the lease to your screen the same day. Unlike paper-and-Excel workflows or overpriced, office-bound legacy production software, GreaseBook runs on the phone your pumper already carries: 8-minute learning curve, turnkey setup, 200% guarantee.

**TinyPumper:** For producers running conventional wells where SCADA never penciled or where aging SCADA costs more to keep alive than it returns, TinyPumper is the remote monitoring system that delivers roughly 99% of SCADA's upside without the cost or complexity. Unlike six-figure SCADA installs or telemetry that needs babysitting, TinyPumper self-installs in 10 minutes, runs solar with cellular/satellite included, one flat rate per site, 60-day money-back with lifetime sensor replacement.

**How the doctrine feeds the value equation** (ties to the Hormozi framework in the sales engine): the two beacons raise the **dream outcome's** contrast; leadership/whole-product proof raises **perceived likelihood of achievement**; "same day" and "10 minutes" attack **time delay**; "the phone he already carries" and "if you can change a lightbulb" attack **effort and sacrifice**.

### GreaseBook vs Legacy Production Software (IHS FieldDirect, WolfePak, Productioneer)

*(List corrected by Greg, 2026-07-14: FieldDirect is the primary named incumbent; iWell removed — it's a modern peer, not legacy. See the incumbent-naming rule in the Positioning Doctrine above.)*

Overarching themes:

- You're just a number to them. They won't give you personalized attention.
- Old, outdated, codebase locked. They are not actively pushing updates.
- Founders have been out of the trenches for too long.
- With GreaseBook, you get personalized attention and a team that ships features based on your feedback.

### TinyPumper vs Legacy SCADA (eLynx, ZDScada, PetroPower, SignalFire)

- SCADA requires IT to maintain, troubleshoot, and update. TinyPumper requires zero IT.
- SCADA has massive upfront costs. TinyPumper is 95% cheaper.
- SCADA maintenance is a hidden drain. TinyPumper swaps like a lightbulb.
- SCADA hardware ages out. TinyPumper is a drop-in replacement.

### TinyPumper vs Modern Remote Monitoring (iWell, Sensorfield, Innotech, Amplified)

- **iWell:** Alerts only fire on the hour. TinyPumper's sensor checks every 5 minutes and fires an alert immediately if thresholds are crossed. Small difference, big consequence on a runaway water tank.
- **Sensorfield / Innotech:** Submersible sensors that corrode, freeze, and foul. TinyPumper uses radar on top of the tank. No fluid contact, no failures.
- **Amplified Industries:** Real moat is their load cell / dyno card (control, not measurement). We don't fight that battle. We flip it: if their basic tank measurements aren't even accurate (phantom drops, bad signals), how can you trust them to control the well? Lead with TinyPumper's measurement reliability, support responsiveness, and price ($79/mo/site vs $155/mo/battery).

See `docs/Sales/TinyPumper_Sales/03_Sales_Reconnaissance.md` for the full competitor file.

### GreaseBook and Accounting Software (both/and, not either/or)

We target keywords like "production allocation software" and "production accounting software" because that is how operators search. We are **not** trying to replace oil and gas accounting platforms, and our copy should never frame it that way.

**Framing rule:** accounting software is not the enemy. Most of our clients run GreaseBook **alongside** their accounting system, and that is the win-win we should be pitching.

Here is the honest picture:

- Oil and gas accounting platforms have their own production modules built in. Those modules exist to serve the accounting workflow, not the field.
- Operators generally view their accounting software as a necessary evil. They tolerate it because the CPA or the back office needs it. They do not love it.
- The production tools bolted on to those accounting suites are **jack of all trades, master of none**. They work if you squint, but they were never built for a pumper in a truck at 5 a.m.
- GreaseBook is purpose-built for production data capture, gauge sheets, allocations, and pumper accountability. Simple, fast, field-first.
- **GreaseBook integrates with all the major oil and gas accounting platforms and engineering / decline-curve tools like PHDwin.** Production data flows in. Accounting does what accounting does. Nobody has to pick a side.
- A lot of operators with working interest partners came to us specifically because things got complex. GreaseBook handles the entire production gathering process cleanly, then hands a clean dataset off to whatever accounting system the operator already runs.

**The pitch, in operator language:** "Keep your accounting software. We don't compete with it. We make it better by feeding it clean production data from the field. You get world-class production software that is simple to use, and it ties right into the accounting system you already pay for."

**Accounting software tiers (know where our buyers actually sit):**

| Tier | Platforms | Well-count fit | Our stance |
|------|-----------|----------------|------------|
| **Mid-range** (where most of our buyers live) | OGsys, Wolfpak, Bolo, SSI, Pac Energy | Operators running ~1,000 wells or fewer | Primary focus. GreaseBook integrates cleanly and solves the production-side pain these tools don't. |
| **Next level up** | P2, Quorum, W Energy | Operators running ~1,000 to 10,000 wells | We work with plenty of these clients too. Bigger operations, same integration story. |
| **Top level** | SAP | Majors and supermajors (not our buyer) | Ludicrous for an oil and gas producer. If someone is running SAP for production, the money-losing overhead alone is a story. We don't compete with it and we don't pretend to. |

**Do not confuse the tiers.** Pac Energy, Wolfpak, OGsys, Bolo, and SSI serve operations in the ~1,000-wells-and-under band — they are not peers of P2 or Quorum. Putting a mid-range platform in the same sentence as P2/Quorum misreads the market and confuses the reader. Keep the tiers separate.

When writing copy, anchor examples to the mid-range tier by default. Do not imply the reader is on P2/Quorum, and never imply they should be on SAP.

**Complexity requires real oil and gas accounting software. Do not push QuickBooks as a substitute.**

Any producing company with real complexity (working interest partners, JIB, multi-lease, royalty owners, AFE management, multi-state tax) needs purpose-built oil and gas accounting software. That is not a niche or a nice-to-have. It is table stakes. Copy should respect that and reflect it:

- **Do not frame operators running OGsys, Wolfpak, Bolo, SSI, P2, or Quorum as doing something wrong or wasteful.** They made the right call. Those are the buyers with resources, process, and scale — they are exactly who we want as clients.
- **Do not position QuickBooks as the "simple" alternative.** Operators still running QuickBooks for oil and gas operations are not ahead of the curve — they are setting themselves up for an audit, a missed JIB, or a compliance headache. If QuickBooks comes up at all, the honest line is that it is a stopgap that stops working the minute working-interest complexity enters the picture.
- **Respect the sophisticated reader.** A company running P2 or Quorum has made deliberate, expensive decisions to handle real operational complexity. Copy that assumes the reader wishes they had something simpler is wrong and alienates the exact buyer we want.
- **Complexity is a GreaseBook unlock, not a disqualifier.** Working interest partners, JIB, multi-lease operations are where GreaseBook's allocation and production-gathering earn their keep — because we clean up the production side of the equation before it ever hits the accounting suite.

The honest positioning: **GreaseBook respects that you need real accounting software for a real oil and gas operation. We make the production side of that equation simple, clean, and field-first, so your accounting system (whatever tier you run) has clean data to work with.**

**Comparison pages — component, not combatant.**

Every comparison page that stacks GreaseBook against an oil and gas accounting platform (W Energy, OGsys, Wolfpak, Bolo, SSI, P2, Quorum) must use the **component** frame, not the head-to-head frame.

- **We are not a replacement. We are a component.** We do the production side. They do the accounting side. We integrate seamlessly into whatever they run.
- **If the page drifts into head-to-head territory (production module vs. GreaseBook), the honest position is simple:** on the production side specifically, GreaseBook is heads-and-tails above the bolt-on production modules these platforms ship. The vendor built a production module as a checkbox for the accounting suite; we built the whole company around production data. But we still integrate with their platform, so it is never either/or.
- **Never write a comparison page that tries to win the accounting side of the fight.** We do not do that job. We do not want that job. The operator will still use [accounting vendor] for accounting.
- **The pitch on a comparison page:** "We integrate seamlessly with [vendor]. On the production side we are heads and tails better than their bolt-on module — because that is the only thing we do. Use both. Why wouldn't you?"
- **Article structure on comparison pages** should show the reader a two-column view: (1) what [accounting vendor] does best (accounting, JIB, revenue distribution, taxes), (2) what GreaseBook does best (field capture, pumper accountability, allocation, state reports, real-time production data). Then show the integration. No scoreboards, no "GreaseBook wins 8-to-3" grids.

**By running GreaseBook alongside their accounting software, an operator:**

1. **Saves money** — they don't have to pay to upgrade to the pricier "production module" tier of their accounting suite, and they stop losing production to invisible downtime.
2. **Saves time** — pumpers are in and out faster, the back office stops re-keying numbers, and month-end reconciliations stop eating entire weekends.
3. **Saves their sanity** — the production side finally works the way it is supposed to, so the accounting software stops being the thing that ruins their week.

**What to say / what to never say:**

| Do not say | Say instead |
|------------|-------------|
| "Ditch your accounting software." | "Keep your accounting software. We make it better." |
| "[Accounting vendor] is garbage." | "[Accounting vendor] is fine for accounting. For production data, they are a jack of all trades, master of none." |
| "Replace your production accounting module." | "Feed your accounting system clean production data from the field." |
| "You don't need [accounting platform]." | "You still need accounting. We just handle the production side better, and it flows straight in." |

If an article, ad, or email knocks the accounting software vendors by name or frames the choice as either/or, rewrite it. Both/and is the only honest positioning.

## 7. Message Pillars for Marketing

When writing a cold email, ad, landing page, or piece of content, pull the angle from one of these pillars. Every message should ladder up to at least one. Every message also passes the two-beacon triangulation check and uses its brand's chasm-stage proof (leadership-and-safety for GreaseBook, triangulation-and-references for TinyPumper). See Positioning Doctrine, Section 6.

### GreaseBook Pillars

1. **End the 2-to-3 week data delay.** If your production data is more than 48 hours old, you are making decisions on stale numbers.
2. **Stop losing production to invisible downtime.** Wells go down between pumper visits. Catch it the same day, not next week.
3. **Automate the back office.** State reports, run tickets, reconciliations. All of it. Your admin goes home on time.
4. **Trust but verify on pumpers.** Geo-fencing confirms every visit. No more kitchen table pumping.
5. **We stand behind it with 200%.** Not a typo. Doesn't work, we pay you double.

### The Switcher Play — GreaseBook for Producers Already Running Production Software (Greg, 2026-07-18)

When the target already runs a production system, the pitch is NOT the paper/Excel story — he left paper years ago. He is solution-aware: he fights his system to get data in, then fights it to get answers out, and the invoice nickel-and-dimes him. His real objection is never the upside; it is the lift. **Every switcher piece is built on the Hormozi value equation with the weight in the denominator.** These are the canonical points — hit them every time; do not re-derive them per piece:

**Value = (Dream Outcome × Perceived Likelihood) ÷ (Time Delay × Effort & Sacrifice)**

| Lever | The points to hit |
|---|---|
| **Effort ↓ (the headline lever)** | The producer's entire job is handing over a login to the existing system. GreaseBook takes care of the rest: our petroleum engineers do the whole conversion — wells, surface equipment, everything needed to start entering data. The producer never lifts a finger. |
| **Effort ↓ (gear + management)** | No laptops to buy, no new gear, nothing for the office to manage. Pumpers run the app on the smartphones they already carry. |
| **Sacrifice ↓ (sunk cost killer)** | **Contract buyout program:** GreaseBook buys out the months remaining on the old provider's contract in exchange for a minimum one-year term plus the bought-out months (5 months left → a 1-year-5-month term). The old contract is never a reason to stay stuck. |
| **Time ↓** | Most operators fully rolled out **within a week**. Pumpers learn it in **about 8 minutes**. Office users 99% proficient in ~20 minutes. |
| **Likelihood ↑ (has GB done this before?)** | 600+ producers, 10,000+ pumpers, **98% rollout success rate**. This is a repeatable process, not a project. |
| **Likelihood ↑ (risk reversal)** | **200% money-back guarantee.** Doesn't work, we pay you double. |
| **Dream Outcome** | Clean, live production data without fighting the system — and without the invoice surprises. |

**Conversion sequencing — say it right (Greg, 2026-07-18):** GreaseBook imports the wells, surface equipment, and everything needed to *start adding data* first. Pumpers give feedback on their routes, the supervisor signs off, and **then** GreaseBook scrubs, cleans, and backfills the historical production and existing records. Never say "we import everything before the first pumper logs in" — that is not the sequence.

**The switcher's felt moments (use these, never marketing labels):** fighting the system to get data in, then fighting it to get answers out; invoice line items he doesn't recognize; support tickets that go nowhere. Remember the standing rule: software owners are **lukewarm, not burned** — they "deal with it." The workaround indicts the design, never the man.

**Canonical execution (2026-07-18):** the E&M advertorial (`greasebook.com/energy-and-mining-magazine-exclusive-feature/`) is the switcher article — it carries every row of the table above. Live ad angles against it: "One-Login Switch" (effort lever) and "Contract Buyout" (sacrifice lever).

### TinyPumper Pillars

1. **SCADA is overkill. TinyPumper is the right-sized answer.** 10 minutes to install, 95% cheaper, no IT required.
2. **No submersibles. No corrosion. No replacements.** Radar on top of the tank. Lifetime replacement anyway.
3. **Flat rate per site. Unlimited sensors.** No per-sensor gotchas. One price covers everything you want to monitor at that location.
4. **Monitor more than tanks.** Pressures, compressor runtime, engine uptime. It is a full site monitor, not a tank gauge.
5. **60 days to try it. We pay the return shipping.** If it doesn't earn its keep, send it back.

### Shared Pillars (Use for Either Product)

1. **Built in the oil patch, by operators, for operators.** 15 years of feedback from the people who actually do the work.
2. **Independent operators first.** 2 to 2,000 wells. Not the majors. Not the supermajors. The ones who built the business with sweat, not stock options.
3. **Petroleum engineers on the help desk.** Not a call center. Not an offshore team.
