## 8. Product Claim Rules

> **Voice, kill list, and craft rules (em dashes, Proper Case, copy length, etc.) live in the brand tone guide:** `docs/Infrastructure/Skills/gb-tp-brand-tone-for-llm.md`. This section covers product claim rules only — what we do and don't say about the products themselves.

- **Never quote per-sensor pricing for TinyPumper.** It is flat rate per lease.
- **Never say "we install it" for TinyPumper.** The client does. Self-install in 8 to 10 minutes.
- **Never say TinyPumper is "a tank monitor."** It monitors pressures, tanks, and runtime.
- **Never say cellular is extra.** It is included.
- **Never use the 6% profit margin stat for TinyPumper.** That is a GreaseBook-only number.
- **Never use the 200% money-back guarantee for TinyPumper.** That is a GreaseBook offer. TinyPumper is a straight 60-day money-back.
- **GreaseBook is a PURE PRODUCTION app. It does NOTHING financial, monetary, or accounting (Greg, 2026-07-12).** Never say GreaseBook tracks profit, profitability, revenue, JIB, disbursements, lifting cost, LOE, money, or "makes/loses money." It tracks PRODUCTION: gauges, run tickets, allocated production by well and lease, decline curves, downtime, and state/partner reports. When a money-adjacent term must appear (e.g. someone searched "production accounting software"), use the both/and integration frame: GreaseBook FEEDS your accounting system clean production data, it never does the accounting itself. Correct swaps: "see profit by lease" -> "see allocated production by well"; "which leases make money" -> "which wells are pulling their weight"; "lose money" -> "lose barrels." **WHY:** GreaseBook literally has no financial features; claiming any is false, invites a compliance/accuracy problem, and muddies the crisp positioning (production layer that feeds whatever accounting you already run). Origin: Claude wrote "See Profit By Lease" / "per-lease profitability" into GB asset-management copy; Greg caught it 2026-07-12. **THE ONE EXCEPTION (Greg, 2026-07-12): the "6-Week, 6% Net Profit Challenge" offer.** Profit language is allowed there and ONLY there — it is the sitewide guarantee (homepage promise section, CTA banner, sidebar, ad-landing/competitor layouts), not a product-capability claim. Greg's reasoning: "more production equals profit... increasing production, decreasing avoidable downtime, and running a leaner operation, we can get you six percent on your bottom line" — the offer describes the business OUTCOME of the production work; the product still does zero financial tracking. Rule of thumb: profit may appear in the guarantee/offer framing; it may NEVER appear as something GreaseBook shows, tracks, or reports.
- **GreaseBook pricing communication — publish the MODEL, never a number or range (Greg, 2026-07-13).** GB has no public price because every operation is different and deals are negotiated (finite TAM — one bad anchor can kill a deal; a range makes every sales call start as a "why am I not at the bottom?" negotiation). The rule: (1) name the UNIT — GB is priced **per well OR per pumper, per month** (per-pumper often fits gas-heavy Northeast and shallow/low-production operations; per-well fits most oil operations); **office and in-house users are ALWAYS free**; (2) name the DRIVERS — **how many wells you run, how many pumpers cover your routes, what you need to track in your operation** — so a quote feels COMPUTED, not arbitrary (people accept computed prices and fight arbitrary ones). NEVER say "modules" (Greg, 2026-07-13: GreaseBook's whole identity is simple — module-menus create decision fatigue and read like the enterprise suites we position against; well-type/complexity folds into "what you need to track"); (3) anchor with a COMPARISON, never a dollar ("a fraction of one pumper-hour per well per month") — equivalence anchors reassure on magnitude without capping sales; (4) the QUIZ QUALIFIES, the CALL delivers the number — **never promise a price after the quiz** (the quiz outcome is a booking page; only sales can quote; promising "get your price, no salesman" then delivering a booking form makes people ANGRY — Greg caught Claude writing exactly this 2026-07-13). Honest framing: "take the 30-second quiz to see if you're a fit; if you are, grab 15 minutes with a real production engineer and walk out with your exact price. No pitch, no pressure."; (5) the 200% guarantee absorbs the price objection. Never write "starting at $X", never a range, never a specific dollar figure for GB. **Two more hard sub-rules (Greg, 2026-07-13):** (a) the model is per-well OR per-pumper — WE choose after qualifying questions; never promise the prospect a dual quote or "priced both ways, take the better deal" (the page's job is to PREP the unit so the number isn't a shock, not to offer a menu); (b) **never signal negotiating room in public copy** ("sharper pencil", "he'll fight for your number", "flexible pricing") — price-takers would have just taken the price; advertising flex converts them into negotiators. Those who want to negotiate will do it unprompted, and that's fine privately. (TinyPumper is different: TP has public-ish pricing language per its own rules — "a few hundred bucks a device," "$2/facility/day," exact pricing after quiz.) Sales-side requirement: quotes must be keyed to the same three drivers so marketing and sales sound like one model.
- **Excel/paper vs legacy-software attack lines (Greg, 2026-07-13 — for LANDERS and homepage, NOT the booking page).** These are two different competitors with two different failure modes; never conflate them. **Excel & paper:** the real pain is no centralized visibility — data never merges into one spot, so you inevitably fall behind; you can't hold pumpers accountable because you can't keep up; when it's time to review, you're unorganized, and staying organized means paying someone for double work. **Legacy production software:** contract lock-in with hefty setup fees; a huge lift for the pumper — days to learn vs GreaseBook's minutes; requires laptops, so the pumper keys data from HOME instead of the field (everyone has a cell phone — no excuse not to enter data standing at the well; GreaseBook works offline). **The GreaseBook flip:** pumpers become MORE PROACTIVE because feedback lives in the field — they review historical comments and well production from the smartphone at the best possible time: on site, standing in front of the well. Placement rule: "dead wells discovered when the run ticket is light" is an Excel/paper problem, not a legacy-software problem. Booking-page rule (same date): the approved/booking page does NOT carry these arguments — post-qualification pages book, they don't sell; comparison content re-opens a debate the funnel already won.
- **Never mention the paper/Excel old way without naming the legacy-software incumbent in the same breath, and vice versa (triangulation rule, Greg, 2026-07-14).** Two beacons, one landing point: the phone the pumper already carries. This COMPOSES with the attack-lines rule directly above: name both together, attack each only with its own failure mode. Same discipline for TinyPumper with its own beacons (flying blind + SCADA/telemetry → self-installed hardware). Never name Pump Pilot. **WHY:** *Crossing the Chasm* — pragmatists buy by triangulating; one beacon leaves an exit toward whichever alternative went unnamed. Full doctrine: Section 6.
- **"Production accounting" refinement (Greg, 2026-07-21 — refines the 2026-07-12 production-only rule, does NOT relax it):** GreaseBook may be framed as a COMPLETE, STANDALONE production accounting suite: run ticket and oil purchaser reconciliation, allocation by well and lease, downtime tracking, all state production reports, management reporting and alerts on production. "You've come to the right place; no bulky, expensive suite required" is approved framing on production-accounting keyword pages. The boundary that never moves: the general accounting FUNCTION (the ledger: billing partners, cutting distributions, JIB, revenue) is a different job GreaseBook deliberately does not do — state that honestly and offer the feed to any accounting tool on the market (allusion pattern). WHY: many operators legitimately need nothing beyond the production side; telling them "we only feed accounting systems" undersold the product on its own keyword (Greg caught it on the /ppc/oil-and-gas-production-accounting-systems/ lander, 2026-07-21). First application: that lander, same day.
- **Never bastardize oil and gas accounting software.** We target "production allocation" and "production accounting" keywords, but we do not compete with accounting platforms. Many clients run GreaseBook alongside their accounting system. Frame it as both/and, not either/or. If the accounting vendors' built-in production tools come up, the honest line is "jack of all trades, master of none" — never a hit piece on the vendor. See Section 6 for the full framing rule.
- **Never alienate horizontal well operators.** GreaseBook serves plenty of horizontal operators and integrates with their SCADA systems. If copy knocks SCADA in a way that reads as "GreaseBook is not for you if you run SCADA," rewrite. TinyPumper's anti-SCADA positioning does not extend to GreaseBook. See Section 1 for the full framing.
- **Never pitch the pumper or contract pumper as the buyer.** For both GreaseBook and TinyPumper, the buyer is the producer (the operating company). Pumpers are users. If copy frames TinyPumper as "for contract pumpers managing multiple operators" or GreaseBook as "a pumper tool," rewrite. See Section 1 bright-line rule.
- **Never gate TinyPumper by well count.** It is not "for small operators" and it is not "the tool you use until you hit 500 wells." It is the SCADA alternative for conventional wells at any scale. The value prop — ~99% of SCADA upside without the cost or complexity — holds for a 50-well operator and a 5,000-well operator. Copy that buckets TinyPumper into a well-count band (e.g., "5 to 50 wells, TinyPumper; 50 to 200, SCADA") is wrong on its face and must be rewritten. See Section 2 well-count-agnostic rule.
- **Quorum rules (refined by Greg, 2026-07-11).** What Quorum actually objected to: advertising the integration and using their logo on our integrations wall. The rules: (1) **never the Quorum logo, anywhere**; (2) **never advertise the GreaseBook–Quorum integration** — Quorum does not appear in integration lists or logo walls (use "and more" / "any other major platform"); (3) never the Quorum name in ad copy (covered by the platform-wide no-trademarks-in-ads rule anyway); (4) **naming Quorum on a landing page for truthful comparison is FINE** (nominative fair use — no affiliation implied, no logo); (5) **bidding on Quorum keyword terms continues** (settled law; trademark owners can restrict ad copy, not keyword targeting). Why we honor the integration-advertising ask beyond legal necessity: cheap diplomacy with a vendor whose ecosystem our clients live in. **The allusion pattern (Greg-approved, 2026-07-11) — how to tell a Quorum shop we integrate without naming Quorum:** category-total claim + named partial list that conspicuously stops short + self-identify invite. House copy: "Greasebook integrates with every major oil and gas accounting platform on the market. WolfePak, OGsys, Bolo, SSI, P2, PHDwin, and the rest of the majors you'd expect. Run something we didn't name? If it's a major platform, we already talk to it — tell us yours on the quiz and we'll confirm on the spot." The reader draws the inference; no name, no logo, no integration advertised. On the phone, say Quorum freely.
- **SSI and P2 are separate systems.** Never write "SSI/P2." Integration lists include PHDwin (engineering/decline curves) alongside the accounting platforms: WolfePak, OGsys, Bolo, SSI, P2, PHDwin.
- **Never run a head-to-head comparison page against an accounting vendor's production module.** We are a component, not a combatant. Comparison pages must use the component frame: we integrate, we handle production, they handle accounting. If the page needs to address the bolt-on production module head-on, the honest line is that we are heads and tails better on the production side specifically — but that is a footnote, not the thesis. See Section 6 comparison-page rule.

---
================================================================================
PART 5 - CLAIMS POLICY
================================================================================

## Audience framing

The audience is always **the oil and gas producing company**. Actors in the workflow (pumper, operator, contractor, field supervisor, accountant) can appear as characters. Do not reframe the audience as "for pumpers" or "for contractors" — those are actors, not the audience.

## Default author (E-E-A-T)

Default author for all blog content is **Greg Archbald, founder of GreaseBook**. Bio line: "Greg Archbald is the founder of GreaseBook. He built the product from inside the oil patch and has spent 15+ years on the operator side of oil and gas technology."

- GreaseBook-led content: Greg Archbald by default.
- TinyPumper-led content: Greg Archbald by default (same founder, different product emphasis). May be overridden by the user for specific posts with a named contractor voice.
- Mixed content: Greg Archbald.
- Never attribute to "GreaseBook Team", "TinyPumper Team", "Editorial Staff", or any anonymous collective — this collapses E-E-A-T.
- Byline must link to a /team/greg-archbald (or equivalent) author page. If the author page does not exist, the architecture record should flag it as a prerequisite.

## Product-fit honesty

Every article declares a primary product fit in the architecture record. The copy, CTA, and proof points must match that declaration.

- GreaseBook-led sections may use GreaseBook-specific proof.
- TinyPumper-led sections must stand on TinyPumper's own proof (or no proof) — never borrow GreaseBook's.
- Mixed articles may use both, but each proof point stays attached to its own product.

## Restricted to GreaseBook-led content

These proof points are GreaseBook-only unless the user provides updated approved proof for TinyPumper:
- 6% pump-to-net improvement in 6 weeks
- 98% success rate
- 200% money-back guarantee
- pumpers trained in under 10 minutes

Never port these to TinyPumper-led sections or TinyPumper CTAs.

## Require proof or source

Do not state numbers, percentages, or comparative outcomes unless they are:
- provided by the user
- already approved in the business context
- traceable to a real public or internal source

## Restricted claim categories

Be careful with:
- SCADA replacement claims
- regulatory or compliance guarantees
- uptime or downtime reduction promises
- ROI claims presented as universal
- competitor performance claims

## Wrong-fit rule

When a page is not a fit for all producing companies, say so directly. Categories that may need a wrong-fit statement:
- high-volume horizontals
- heavy SCADA environments
- enterprise ERP-led workflows
- producing companies with in-house developed tools

A wrong-fit statement builds trust and improves conversion on the visitors who are the right fit.

## Audience inclusivity — no gatekeeping anchors

Do not anchor scene-setting or example copy to a single basin, a single well-count, or a single operator archetype. Lines like "a 50-well operation in the Permian" or "a 200-well operator in West Texas" read as copy-deck flavor to the writer, but they quietly tell every other reader — a 20-well operator in Oklahoma, a 300-well operator in Pennsylvania, a 15-well operator in California — that this article is not for them. They bounce.

Rules:
- **Name ranges, not single numbers.** "15 to 500 wells", "a dozen stripper wells to a few hundred", "small and mid-size independents" all work.
- **Name basins in plural, or skip basin entirely.** If you name one basin, name several ("Texas, Oklahoma, North Dakota, California, Pennsylvania"), or go basin-agnostic with "anywhere oil and gas gets produced in the United States".
- **Let the reader self-select.** The best copy shows the reader their own operation in the example without ever naming their specific geography or headcount.
- **Exception:** a page that genuinely is geo- or size-scoped (e.g., a Texas RRC filings pillar, a stripper-well specific page) should anchor — but that anchor must match the target keyword, not be incidental scene-dressing.

## Product-category honesty — allocation has two jobs

Production allocation is widely mis-framed as "only for operators with outside partners or complex working interest structures." That framing is wrong and it excludes a real buyer. Allocation has two jobs, both of which matter independently:

1. **Revenue splitting** — needed when there are outside partners, multiple leases, or royalty owners. This is the obvious one.
2. **Per-well productivity testing on shared tank batteries** — needed any time two or more wells feed a common tank battery, even when the operator owns 100% of every barrel. Without allocation, the tank reading tells you the battery's total production. With allocation (run against monthly well tests), you catch the well that has been loafing for three months while the good wells carry the battery.

Both jobs should appear in any article that defines or positions allocation. Do not write copy that says "you do not need allocation because there is nothing to allocate" — that denies the productivity-testing use case and excommunicates the operator whose real pain is not knowing which well is underperforming.

The honest nuance: for small operations with a handful of wells on one battery, a spreadsheet built around monthly well tests handles the productivity job. Dedicated allocation software earns its keep when the combinatorics get ugly (multiple batteries, varying ownership, multi-lease). "You may not need allocation software yet" is different from "you may not need allocation" — respect that distinction.

## State reports — ANY oil and gas producing state, never a fixed list (updated 2026-07-11)

GreaseBook auto-files state production reports for **any oil and gas producing state**. On the rare chance a state's form isn't already built, GreaseBook **builds it at no cost to the operator** — Greg: "if you need it, there's a good chance somebody else is going to need it." The free-build promise is what makes the any-state claim honest.

**Copy rules:**

- Standard line: "auto-filed state production reports for any oil and gas producing state," plus the free-build promise where space allows.
- **NEVER enumerate a short list of states as the coverage.** Naming TX/MS/AL/WY/MI reads as "we don't do Kansas/Oklahoma/Colorado" by negative space — exclusion by omission in the reader's mind (Greg, 2026-07-11; supersedes the 2026-04-19 rule that required naming the five-state list).
- Geo-scoped pages (a Texas RRC PR pillar) may anchor to that state's form but must carry the any-state line, not a list of other states.
- Module 7 fail condition updates accordingly: fail a state-reporting article that ENUMERATES a fixed state list as the coverage, or that omits the any-state framing.

## Accounting software positioning — both/and, never either/or

We target keywords like "production allocation software" and "production accounting software" because that is how operators search. We do **not** compete with oil and gas accounting platforms, and SEO copy must never frame it that way.

**The honest picture:**

- Oil and gas accounting suites have production modules bolted on. Those modules serve the accounting workflow, not the field. The buyer landscape has tiers:
  - **Mid-range (where most of our buyers sit):** OGsys, PakEnergy, Bolo, SSI. Operators running ~1,000 wells or fewer. Primary focus for examples, comparisons, and integration language.
  - **Next level up:** P2, Quorum (see Quorum rules below — never in integration lists), W Energy. Operators running ~1,000 to 10,000 wells. We work with plenty of clients on these too.
  - **Top level:** SAP. Majors and supermajors — not our buyer. Ludicrous for an oil and gas producer. Do not position GreaseBook as a peer to or replacement for SAP; do not imply the reader should be on SAP. If SAP comes up at all, the honest line is that it is overkill for a producer.
- **Never collapse the tiers.** PakEnergy, OGsys, Bolo, and SSI are mid-range (≤1,000 wells). Putting them in the same sentence or comparison band as P2/Quorum/W Energy misreads the market and alienates both audiences. Keep them separate.
- Operators view their accounting software as a necessary evil. They tolerate it. They do not love it.
- The bolt-on production tools are **jack of all trades, master of none** — functional if you squint, never built for a pumper in a truck at 5 a.m.
- GreaseBook is purpose-built for production data capture, pumper accountability, allocations, and field-first workflows. It **integrates with every major oil and gas accounting platform** and engineering / decline-curve tools like PHDwin. Production data flows in, accounting does what accounting does.
- Many clients with working interest partners came to GreaseBook specifically because things got complex. GreaseBook handles the production gathering cleanly, then hands a clean dataset off to whatever accounting system the operator already runs.

**Rules for copy:**

- Never say "replace your accounting software" or "ditch [vendor]".
- Never name-and-shame a specific accounting vendor as broken or useless.
- When the accounting vendors' production modules come up, the honest line is "jack of all trades, master of none" — directed at the *category of bolt-on production tools*, never at the vendor as a whole.
- Frame every mention as additive: GreaseBook runs alongside the accounting system, feeds it clean production data, makes the accounting side less painful.
- If the article is commercial-intent on "production accounting software" or "production allocation software" keywords, lead with the integration promise, not a takedown.

**Complexity requires real oil and gas accounting software. Do not push QuickBooks as a substitute.**

Any producing company with real complexity (working interest partners, JIB, multi-lease, royalty owners, AFE management, multi-state tax) needs purpose-built oil and gas accounting software. SEO copy must respect that:

- Operators running OGsys, PakEnergy, Bolo, SSI, P2, or Quorum made the right call. They are the buyers with resources, process, and scale, and they are exactly who we want as clients. Never frame them as over-engineered or wasteful.
- **Quorum rules (Greg, 2026-07-11):** never the Quorum logo; never advertise the GreaseBook–Quorum integration (Quorum stays OUT of integration lists and logo walls — use "and more"); never the name in ad copy. Naming Quorum in article text for truthful comparison or factual reference is fine (nominative fair use). Their actual objection was integration advertising + logo use, not the name itself.
- **SSI and P2 are separate systems — never write "SSI/P2."** Integration lists include PHDwin alongside the accounting platforms.
- Do not position QuickBooks as the "simple" alternative. Operators still running QuickBooks for oil and gas operations are not ahead of the curve — they are setting themselves up for an audit, a missed JIB, or a compliance headache. If QuickBooks comes up, treat it as a stopgap that stops working the minute working-interest complexity enters the picture.
- Respect the sophisticated reader. Copy that assumes the reader wishes they had something simpler alienates the exact buyer we want.
- Complexity is a GreaseBook unlock, not a disqualifier. JIB, working-interest partners, multi-lease — that is where GreaseBook's allocation and production-gathering earn their keep, because we hand clean production data to whatever accounting tier the operator runs.

## Vendor naming — one vendor, one name (Greg, 2026-09-08)

WolfePak, PakAccounting, and PakEnergy are the SAME company. WolfePak was the name before they sold, PakEnergy is the name now, and PakAccounting is its accounting module. Treating them as separate vendors is the most common factual error this corpus has made.

- Canonical name is **PakEnergy**. Never Wolfpak, Wolfpack, Wolfe Pak, Pac Energy, or "Pak Energy" with a space.
- The industry still says WolfePak, and operators who say PakEnergy are usually new to the game, so both names ride together ONCE per article, side by side, on first mention: **PakEnergy (formerly WolfePak)**. PakEnergy alone after that. Keep the gloss out of H2s (they map to LLM sub-queries) and out of JSON-LD (schema text stays stable).
- **Never list the vendor twice in one series.** "OGsys, WolfePak, Bolo, SSI, Pak Energy" names one company at both ends of the same list. It reads to an operator as two products and inflates the apparent field.
- Sub-products keep their own names and are not duplicates: PakEnergy Accounting, PakEnergy Allocate, Pak Land, Scout FDC.

**WHY:** Greg caught the double listing on `/blog/oil-and-gas-accounting-software/` on 2026-09-08, where the vendor rundown carried a WolfePak bullet and a PakAccounting bullet back to back. The mid-range tier list in THIS FILE was the source. It read "OGsys, Wolfpak, Bolo, SSI, Pac Energy" and every draft copied it forward. 80 lines across 25 posts had to be repaired.

**Enforced:** `.github/scripts/vendor_name_gate.py` in `greasebook-deploy` blocks the Pages deploy on any legacy spelling, a bare WolfePak outside the gloss, or the vendor listed twice in one comma series.

## SSI — name it as the PakEnergy alternative (Greg, 2026-09-08)

SSI (www.ebassi.com) is a mid-range oil and gas accounting platform and a direct PakEnergy competitor. Wherever an article names PakEnergy in an accounting context, name SSI too: an alternative operators have had a lot of success with, extremely comprehensive, and its Well History profitability reporting tracks per-well profit trends on a rolling twelve months, which is unmatched among oil and gas accounting systems. The capability is sourceable to SSI's own Oil & Gas Operations page (Well History Reporting, the Annual Well History Report's rolling twelve months of profit trend analysis, multi-level profitability tracking).

SSI is an accounting platform, so it is an alternative to PakEnergy Accounting only. It does not compete with Scout FDC (field capture), PakEnergy Allocate, or Pak Land. Do not offer it as an alternative to those.

**Do not link it.** Vendors are named in text and linked only on pages that already link out to other tools. A lone vendor link reads as an endorsement, and at corpus scale identical links to one domain read as a paid-link footprint. Same gate enforces this.

**Comparison pages — component, not combatant.**

Any comparison page that stacks GreaseBook against an oil and gas accounting platform (W Energy, OGsys, PakEnergy, Bolo, SSI, P2, Quorum) must use the **component frame**, not the head-to-head frame:

- We are not a replacement. We are a component. We do the production side. They do the accounting side. We integrate with whatever they run.
- Do not create head-to-head comparison pages. Do not write "GreaseBook vs [vendor]" scoreboards.
- If the page needs to address the vendor's bolt-on production module head-on, the honest line is: on the production side specifically, GreaseBook is heads and tails above bolt-on production modules, because production data capture is the only thing we do. But that is a footnote, not the thesis. The thesis is integration.
- **Article structure on comparison pages:** show a two-column view — (1) what [accounting vendor] does best (accounting, JIB, revenue distribution, taxes), (2) what GreaseBook does best (field capture, pumper accountability, allocation, state reports, real-time production data). Then show the integration.
- **The pitch line:** "We integrate seamlessly with [vendor]. On the production side we are heads and tails better than their bolt-on module. Use both. Why wouldn't you?"

## Horizontal operators — not alienated

GreaseBook serves a meaningful number of horizontal well operators and does it well. Copy must never imply GreaseBook is "for stripper / vertical ops only."

- GreaseBook integrates with SCADA. Horizontal operators running SCADA on their best wells plug GreaseBook into the same environment. Field-entered data, SCADA-sourced data, and exec dashboards live in one screen.
- Inside a horizontal op: GreaseBook lives alongside SCADA; it does not try to replace it.
- TinyPumper's anti-SCADA positioning is correct for TinyPumper, but it does **not** extend to GreaseBook and does not mean horizontal operators are unwelcome. Horizontal operators who want simple centralized production data use GreaseBook on top of SCADA.
- If the copy knocks SCADA in a way that could read as "GreaseBook is not for you if you run SCADA," rewrite. GreaseBook is absolutely for them.
- In article examples and scene-setting, avoid anchors that excommunicate horizontals ("small stripper operator", "marginal wells only"). Use ranges and mixed well-type language.

**The three wins to cite when explaining the both/and positioning:**

1. Save money — no need to pay for the pricier "production module" tier of the accounting suite; stop losing production to invisible downtime.
2. Save time — pumpers in and out faster; back office stops re-keying; month-end reconciliations stop eating weekends.
3. Save their sanity — production finally works the way it should, so the accounting side stops being the thing that ruins their week.

## Cross-product rule

When mentioning the sibling product in a mixed or single-product article:
- mention the other product only when it genuinely serves the producing company's journey
- do not force sibling-product mentions for link-equity reasons
- explain why the sibling product appears (example: "if the pumper you work with is a contractor managing multiple operators, TinyPumper may be the direct tool they use...")
- link to the sibling product's site, not a blog post, when the mention is product-fit relevant
================================================================================
PART 6 - EDITORIAL STANCE
================================================================================

The blog has a point of view. Every article should reflect one or more of these positions where the topic calls for it. A safe, neutral article is not top-1% content.

These stances are what separate GreaseBook content from generic oil and gas software content.

## 1. Paper tickets are the enemy
Paper gauge sheets, paper run tickets, and paper production reports lose data, cost hours at month-end, and drag down lease value by hiding the real numbers. Any article that touches production reporting should treat paper as the problem being solved, not a legitimate alternative.

## 2. Pumpers should be productive in minutes, not days
If production software takes more than a few minutes for a pumper to learn, it is built wrong. Adoption failure is a design failure, not a training failure. Long rollouts are a vendor problem disguised as a customer problem.

## 3. Enterprise ERP does not fit independent operators
Quorum, P2, Enertia, PakEnergy and the rest are built for majors and priced like it. Independent operators running stripper wells and small-to-mid-size lease operations need something shaped for their reality: mobile-first, offline-capable, fast to deploy, not six-figure implementations.

## 4. SCADA is overkill for most stripper operations
Remote monitoring hardware makes sense on high-value, high-volume wells. For the thousands of stripper wells producing a few barrels a day, the math does not work. Mobile-first data capture by the pumper is the right answer for low-volume, high-scatter well counts.

## 5. Spreadsheets cost more than they save
The "free" Excel workflow costs real money in month-end reconciliation, data errors, version control, and missed barrels. Producing companies that count cost by software license price are counting the wrong thing.

## 6. Monitoring hardware should be right-sized, not enterprise-sized
Producers running conventional wells get priced out of visibility because SCADA never penciled, or they are paying more to keep aging SCADA alive than it returns. That is why TinyPumper exists as a separate product: roughly 99% of SCADA's upside without the cost or the complexity, at any scale. Articles touching remote monitoring should treat the cost-and-complexity math as the real dividing line, not well count.

**The buyer is the producer, always (Greg, offer guide Section 1).** Pumpers and contract pumpers are *users* of TinyPumper; the producing company buys it and signs the check. Never frame TinyPumper as "the contract pumper's tool" or as a product for pumpers juggling multiple operators.

**WHY this changed (2026-09-11):** this stance previously read "Contract pumpers need their own tool... that is why TinyPumper exists," which directly contradicted the bright-line buyer rule in `gb-tp-offer-overview-guide-for-llm.md` Section 1 and the well-count-agnostic rule in Section 2. The offer guide is newer and Greg-confirmed, so it wins. Any content written off the old stance aimed at the wrong buyer.

## 7. Offline-first is non-negotiable in the oil patch
If an app stops working when cell signal drops, it stops working where it matters most. Cloud-only tools fail on the lease. Offline sync is a requirement, not a feature.

## How to apply this stance

- Pick the 1–3 stances most relevant to the article and let them shape the opinion, framing, and comparisons.
- Do not list them as bullet points in the copy. Write from them.
- If an article genuinely has no position, reconsider whether it should exist.
- Wrong-fit statements often flow directly from these stances (see SKILL.md Module 6).
================================================================================
PART 7 - IMAGERY
================================================================================

## Operating rule

Before placing any image, answer one question:

**"What confusion does this image remove?"**

If the answer is "none," cut it. This is the test that replaces gut feel and the reason decorative AI art keeps getting rejected at QA.

Every image must pass a second test: name its job as **explain**, **compare**, or **prove**. If it does not do one of those three, it does not ship.

## Teaching-value hierarchy

Ranked by information-per-pixel. Higher ranks beat lower ranks for the same slot.

1. **Explanatory diagrams** — highest teaching value
2. **Comparison visuals** — decision-content leverage
3. **Step-by-step process visuals** — procedural clarity
4. **Annotated conceptual illustrations** — abstraction-to-concrete bridge
5. **Data charts** — proof, only when the data is the argument
6. **Decorative AI renders** — not a style, a failure mode

Rank 6 is not an "AI art" category in general. It is specifically: stock-looking futuristic person at a laptop, cinematic drone-over-rig sunset, glossy 3D pumper tablet shot, surreal oilfield scene with no labels. These read as paid ad creative, not editorial content, and oilfield operators read them as agency-produced filler.

## When each type is correct

### Explanatory diagrams

- **Use when**: explaining how a system works, showing relationships between parts, or making an abstract concept concrete
- **Examples**: pipeline diagrams, before/after architecture, decision trees, annotated flowcharts, layered system visuals
- **Oilfield subjects**: field-data-to-allocation-to-partner-statement flow; pumper-to-cloud sync path; SCADA + GreaseBook integration topology; horizontal well with data layers labeled; TinyPumper dispatch-to-ticket-to-audit path
- **Why it works**: high information density; forces scroll-stop; reinforces memory better than decoration; the first image that gets LLM-cited because labels are parseable

### Comparison visuals

- **Use when**: the reader is evaluating options, methods, or vendors
- **Examples**: manual vs automated side-by-side, legacy vs modern, reactive vs predictive, before/after workflow
- **Oilfield subjects**: paper gauge sheet vs mobile app intake; spreadsheet allocation vs GreaseBook allocation; contract-pumper coordination with vs without TinyPumper; SCADA-only vs SCADA + field-data hybrid; QuickBooks-stopgap vs real O&G accounting + GreaseBook production
- **Why it works**: decision content earns longer attention; comparison structure is inherently scannable; supports conversion intent; matches the "decision table" technique from `references/engagement-techniques.md` in visual form

### Step-by-step process visuals

- **Use when**: the post is procedural or describes a transformation over time
- **Examples**: 3-step implementation sequence, problem → intervention → outcome, checklist rendered as a visual path
- **Oilfield subjects**: onboarding a new pumper (day 1 → day 10 → day 30); allocation close process; state-report filing sequence (any producing state; anchor to the page's own state, never a fixed list); alert-to-action timeline; partner statement close
- **Why it works**: reduces cognitive load; creates natural pacing; keeps readers moving through long pillars

### Annotated conceptual illustrations

- **Use when**: the concept is real but not visually obvious, and a full schematic would be overkill
- **Examples**: "data moving through a field operations stack" with labeled components; "fragmented operations" with labeled failure points; isometric well-pad with data callouts
- **Oilfield subjects**: tank battery with allocation callouts; gauge-to-ticket-to-partner-statement path; horizontal well with SCADA + field-data layers labeled; well-pad-level alert routing
- **Why it works**: more engaging than a sterile chart, still explanatory when annotated; best fit for hero slots on pillars where a pure diagram would feel cold

### Data charts (only when the data is the argument)

- **Use when**: the claim depends on real numbers, trends, or deltas, and credibility matters
- **Examples**: line charts, bar comparisons, benchmark plots, cost/time reduction charts
- **Oilfield subjects**: pump-to-net improvement timeline (GreaseBook pillars only — 6% stat is GB-only); labor hours before/after; allocation-error rate; state-report filing time; days-to-close-month
- **Guardrail**: do not use charts to look smart. Low-signal charts waste attention. If you cannot name the number the chart proves, cut it. Fewer than 3 data points = turn it into a sentence.
- **Hard rule**: **never generate data charts with an image model.** AI image models hallucinate axes and numbers. Use Datawrapper, Flourish, or hand-authored SVG from real numbers. AI-rendered "charts" are an automatic FAIL in Module 7.

## Design traits (non-negotiable)

- one concept per visual (not three)
- obvious focal point
- minimal clutter
- **labels integrated into the image** — captions cannot do the teaching
- consistent perspective and icon vocabulary across the blog
- readable typography at 600–800px blog width
- strong contrast; legible on light and dark renderings
- enough whitespace to parse in 2–3 seconds

**Hard rule**: if an image needs a paragraph to explain the image, the image failed.

## Style kit (site-wide consistency)

A blog needs a visual system, not one-off images. Lock these once and reuse across every post:

- **Illustration style**: isometric or editorial flat-vector — pick one, stick with it
- **Palette**: neutral base + one brand accent. **GreaseBook teal `#51A69D`** for GreaseBook-led content; **TinyPumper gold `#C8993B`** for TinyPumper-led content. **Never both in the same image** — it confuses product emphasis. (Corrected 2026-09-11: this line read "GreaseBook orange" for months. GreaseBook has never been orange on any surface. Exact tokens live in `Mission_Control/docs/Infrastructure/Skills/greasebook-design-system.md` and `tinypumper-design-system.md`, which own the palettes; do not restate hexes elsewhere.)
- **Icon vocabulary**: consistent shapes for well, tank, pumper, dashboard, mobile app, partner statement, SCADA unit, ticket, gauge. Define once; reuse.
- **Typography in images**: one sans-serif, two sizes max, readable at 600px width
- **Photography vs illustration**: real oilfield photography is preferred over AI-rendered "oilfield scenes" when available. AI-rendered rigs and pumpers drift into uncanny territory and erode credibility with operators who know what a real lease looks like.

## Prompt templates

Replace bracketed fields. All prompts assume a restrained editorial style, not glossy stock. Paste the body of the relevant block into the `--prompt` flag of the CLI above.

### Explanatory diagram

```
Isometric technical diagram, clean vector style, muted neutral palette
with one [brand accent color] accent, labeled components, minimal
clutter, showing: [subject — e.g., "pumper gauges tank, submits data
via mobile app, data syncs to cloud dashboard, partner statement
generated"]. Labels integrated into the illustration with thin leader
lines. White or light background. No photorealism. No stock-art figures.
```

### Comparison visual

```
Side-by-side comparison illustration, editorial flat-vector style,
two panels separated by a vertical divider. Left panel: [legacy state
— e.g., "paper tickets, scattered spreadsheets, frustrated pumper"].
Right panel: [improved state — e.g., "mobile app, single dashboard,
clear partner statement"]. Each element labeled. Consistent perspective
and palette across both panels. Neutral background.
```

### Step-by-step process

```
Horizontal three-step process illustration, numbered nodes connected
by arrows, flat-vector editorial style. Step 1: [state]. Step 2:
[action]. Step 3: [outcome]. Each step labeled and captioned underneath.
One [brand accent] for active-node highlight. Clean light background.
```

### Annotated conceptual illustration

```
Annotated cutaway illustration, isometric perspective, showing
[subject — e.g., "tank battery with three lease lines, allocation
meter, and partner statement output"]. Callout labels with thin
leader lines to each component. Editorial flat-vector style. Muted
palette with one [brand accent] for labels.
```

### Summary framework / decision map

```
Decision map illustration, flat-vector editorial style, branching
tree layout. Root node: [question — e.g., "Do you share tank batteries
across wells?"]. Two or three branches with labeled outcomes. One
[brand accent] for the recommended path. Clean background, readable
at 600px width.
```

### What not to prompt

- "futuristic AI oilfield" — purely decorative, no teaching content
- "cinematic drone shot of a well pad at sunset" — mood, not information
- "3D render of a pumper looking at a tablet" — stock aesthetic, no labels
- "surreal abstract representation of data flowing through pipes" — interpretive, not explanatory
- any prompt that does not name labeled components, a specific comparison, or a specific step sequence

These prompts are the direct cause of most Module 7 imagery FAILs. If the prompt reads like an ad concept, the image will too.

## Oilfield subject library

Pre-approved subjects keyed to GreaseBook and TinyPumper content. Pull from this list in Module 6 briefs; extend only when a pillar genuinely needs a new subject.

### GreaseBook-led

- pumper-to-cloud data sync (mobile app → dashboard)
- tank battery with allocation callouts (shared-battery allocation)
- field-data-to-partner-statement path
- state-report filing flow (anchor to the page's own state form, e.g. TX RRC PR; never a fixed five-state list)
- daily production reporting timeline (yesterday's numbers → today's decisions)
- integration topology with O&G accounting (OGsys / PakEnergy / Bolo / SSI / P2 / Quorum / W Energy as integration partners, not competitors)
- horizontal well with SCADA + GreaseBook field-data layers labeled
- pumper onboarding timeline (under-10-minute training claim — GB-only)
- well-pad-level alert routing

### TinyPumper-led

- SCADA-alternative coverage map (per-well visibility without SCADA capital)
- self-install sequence (gateway, radar tank sensor, pressure sensor, 10 minutes)
- solar gateway with up to 8 sensors over Bluetooth, cellular or satellite uplink
- what the producer sees between pumper visits (tank level, pressure, runtime, on one timeline)
- threshold-crossing alert path (sensor wakes, gateway pushes, phone lights up)
- legacy SCADA maintenance drag vs drop-in replacement
- route planning from live site status (which leases need attention today, which can be skipped)
- radar-on-top-of-tank vs submersible (no fluid contact, no corrosion, no freezing)

**Buyer rule for every TinyPumper visual (2026-09-11):** the subject is the **producer's** operation and the producer's economics. Pumpers may appear as characters in the scene, never as the customer. The previous list here ("contract-pumper dispatch board", "route optimization across a contract-pumper's operators", "price/invoice workflow for contract pumpers") framed the contract pumper as the buyer, which contradicts the bright-line rule in `gb-tp-offer-overview-guide-for-llm.md` Section 1 and has been replaced.

### Shared (either product depending on emphasis)

- workflow bottleneck diagram (manual → automated)
- alert-to-action process
- month-end close timeline
- before/after operational comparison

## Accessibility and technical requirements

- **alt text**: mandatory on every image. Describe the **teaching job**, not the subject. "Image of well pad" fails. "Pumper's mobile app syncing daily gauge data to a cloud dashboard, with the partner statement generated downstream" passes.
- **file format**: SVG for diagrams and charts (scales cleanly, small file); WebP for photography; PNG for illustrations with embedded text (preserves text rendering)
- **dimensions**: deliver at 1600px wide, display at 800px for retina crispness
- **ImageObject JSON-LD**: pillar hero images get structured data (see `references/schema-templates.md`)
- **lazy loading**: everything below the first body visual
- **file naming**: `slug-imagetype-subject.ext` — e.g., `production-allocation-software-diagram-tank-battery.svg`. Helps Google Images match the image to the page's topic.

## FAIL triggers (feed Module 7)

Fail the draft if any of these are true:

- **decorative image on a pillar or comparison page** — a hero or body image whose teaching job cannot be named as explain / compare / prove
- **stock-style AI render on a pillar hero** — glossy person-at-laptop, surreal cinematic scene, oilfield-sunset drone shot, or any image that is aesthetic without being instructive
- **AI-generated data chart** — charts must come from real numbers via a chart tool (Datawrapper / Flourish / hand-authored SVG), not from an image model. AI chart renders hallucinate data and are an automatic fail.
- **image plan missing from pillar or comparison brief** — Module 6 requires a named plan per image slot; "we'll add hero later" is not a plan
- **alt text absent or generic** — "image of well" fails; alt text must describe the teaching job
- **image requires a paragraph to explain itself** — the image failed its job
- **style drift** — illustration style, palette, or icon vocabulary inconsistent with the rest of the blog
- **mixed brand accent on the same image** — GreaseBook teal and TinyPumper gold in one visual; confuses product emphasis
- **cross-product proof-point leakage in imagery** — GreaseBook-only stat (6% pump-to-net, 98% success rate, 200% money-back) visualized on a TinyPumper-led page
- **single-basin or single-well-count visual anchor** — a hero scene labeled "Permian 50-well operator" violates the audience-inclusivity rule in `references/claims-policy.md`. Name ranges or skip the anchor.
- **accounting-vendor hit-piece imagery** — a visual that pits GreaseBook head-to-head against an O&G accounting platform's production module violates the comparison-pages rule in `references/claims-policy.md`. Use the integration/component frame in visual form too.

### Borderline (flag, not fail)

- more than 5 images on a 2000-word pillar
- hero is a photo when the concept is abstract (a diagram would teach better)
- chart with fewer than 3 data points (probably should be a sentence)
- decorative hero on a **supporting article** (not ideal, but not pillar-grade content so it does not block publish)
================================================================================
PART 8 - THE OTHER BRAND
================================================================================

## 4. Color

The brand lives on a near-black and off-white spine with a single teal accent. There is no secondary accent. Restraint is the point: teal only ever marks the thing you want the reader to act on or notice.

### Tokens (exact, from the homepage `:root`)

| Token | Hex | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--accent` | `#51A69D` | The teal. CTAs, links, icons, emphasis, map pins, the "with GreaseBook" column |
| `--accent-hover` | `#448F87` | Button and link hover |
| `--accent-glow` | `rgba(81,166,157,0.15)` | Soft teal wash behind accent elements |
| `--bg-dark` / `--text-dark` | `#0F1114` | Dark section background. Primary text on light. |
| `--bg-dark-card` | `#1A1D23` | Cards and panels inside dark sections |
| `--bg-light` / `--text-light` | `#FAFAF9` | Light section background. Text on dark. |
| `--bg-light-alt` | `#F3F2EF` | Alternate light panel, feature cards |
| `--text-muted-dark` | `#9CA3AF` | Secondary text on dark |
| `--text-muted-light` | `#6B7280` | Secondary text on light |
| `--red-muted` | `#DC2626` | The "without GreaseBook" column, the old way, warnings |
| `--red-bg` | `rgba(220,38,38,0.08)` | Fill behind the "without" column |
| `--green-bg` | `rgba(81,166,157,0.08)` | Fill behind the "with" column |
| `--border-dark` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.08)` | Hairlines on dark |
| `--border-light` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.08)` | Hairlines on light |
| Star gold | `#F59E0B` | Review stars only. Not a brand accent. |

### Two teals are in production, on purpose

Logo art is `#22A89D`. UI accent is `#51A69D`.

- **Build everything with `#51A69D`.** It is the token the entire site and blog run on.
- **Use `#22A89D` only when reproducing the logo** or matching artwork to the mark.
- Do not "correct" one to the other in existing assets.

### Rules

- **One accent.** Teal is the only accent in a GreaseBook layout. Red appears only in before/after contrast and warnings. Gold appears only as review stars.
- **Never use TinyPumper gold (`#C8993B`) in a GreaseBook layout.** Two brands, two systems.
- **Never put two brand accents in one image.** It confuses which product the piece is about.
- Dark and light sections alternate down the page. That rhythm is the layout, not decoration. Hero is dark. Final CTA is dark.
- Reference every color as a CSS custom property. Never hardcode a hex inline.

---

## 5. Typography

Two families do all the work. There is no third font.

| Family | Weights | Role | Fallback |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DM Serif Display** | 400 only | All headings (h1 to h3), pull quotes, big numbers in stat blocks | `Georgia, serif` |
| **DM Sans** | 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, plus italic 400 | Body, UI, buttons, labels, nav, captions | `-apple-system, sans-serif` |

Google Fonts load:

```
https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=DM+Sans:ital,opsz,wght@0,9..40,300;0,9..40,400;0,9..40,500;0,9..40,600;0,9..40,700;1,9..40,400&family=DM+Serif+Display&display=swap
```

### Scale

| Element | Setting |
|---|---|
| Body | `17px` / line-height `1.7` / DM Sans 400 |
| h1 | `clamp(2.2rem, 5vw, 3.6rem)` / 400 / `1.2` / letter-spacing `-0.02em` |
| h2 | `clamp(1.8rem, 3.5vw, 2.6rem)` / 400 / `1.2` / letter-spacing `-0.01em` / margin-bottom `32px` |
| h3 | `clamp(1.1rem, 2vw, 1.35rem)` / 400 / margin-bottom `12px` |
| Kicker | `12px` / DM Sans 700 / uppercase / letter-spacing `0.14em` / accent color |
| Micro copy | `14px` / muted token |
| Stats strip | `14px` / DM Sans 700 / muted / `5px` teal dot separators |

### Rules

- **DM Serif Display has one weight (400). Never fake-bold it.** If a heading needs more presence, make it bigger, not heavier.
- **Max sans weight is 700.** No 800, no 900.
- **Emphasis in body copy is bold DM Sans (600/700), not teal type.** Teal is for links and UI, never for coloring words inside a paragraph. (The "bold the key phrases" rule itself is owned by the brand tone guide.)
- **Headings are sentence case** and carry a full stop when they are a full sentence. The homepage h1 is the standing exception.
- Italic DM Sans 400 is for the promise line and map subtitle only.
